, ağır yüklerin güverte veya ambar taban: It ensures that the pressure exerted by heavy loads on the deck or hatch floor remains within permissible limits. Deck load capacity is usually expressed in tonnes/m² and load distribution is optimized by using dunnage (wooden pads).
, ağırlık merkezi ile kaldırma kuvvetini: represents the horizontal distance between the center of gravity and the direction of the buoyant force. A positive GZ indicates that the ship has righting capability.
, ağırlık merkezinin düşey konumunu kont: It aims to keep the vertical position of the center of gravity under control. According to this principle, during loading, the lower tanks and holds are filled first, and the tanks at the upper level are filled last. In the emptying process, this order is reversed: first the upper tanks are emptied, then the lower tanks are moved. This approach ensures that KG remains at the lowest possible level in all intermediate cases and prevents the value of GM from falling to critical levels.
, belirli bir süre için geçerli olan değ: , are changes that are valid for a certain period of time. This includes a temporarily removed buoy, temporary work area or short-term restrictions. It is clearly displayed on the chart as temporary and is removed when it expires.
, boyuna mukavemet açısından kritik sena: are critical scenarios in terms of longitudinal strength. Hogging is the upward bending of the middle part of the ship and usually occurs with heavy loading at the bow and stern and light loading in the middle. Sagging is the downward bending of the middle part and occurs in cases of heavy loading in the middle and light loading in the bow and stern. These situations can exceed the ship's shear force and bending moment limits and cause structural damage.

, geminin boyuna kesit boyunca kesme kuv: calculates shear force and bending moment diagrams along the longitudinal section of the ship. These values are compared with the limit values determined by the classification society and a warning is given in case of exceedance. It is critical that the loading sequence does not exceed the longitudinal strength limits, especially on ships such as bulk carriers and tankers.
, geminin bulunduğu hattı verir: gives the line where the ship is located
, geminin hiçbir kargo, yakıt, tatlı su: refers to the situation where the ship does not carry any cargo, fuel, fresh water or consumables and floats only with its structural weight. Lightship weight includes the steel structure of the ship's hull, fixed machinery and equipment, paint, insulation materials and fixed ballast. Lightship displacement and KG value are determined experimentally by inclining experiment and form the reference point for all subsequent stability calculations. Lightship values may vary depending on the ship's structural modifications; Therefore, after significant modifications, the inclining test must be renewed or the weight calculation must be made.
, geminin küçük bir yatma sonrası kendil: is the situation in which the ship tends to spontaneously return to its upright position after a small heel. In this case, when the ship is tilted, the center of lift shifts to such a position relative to the center of gravity that a righting moment occurs. This moment returns the ship to its initial position. This is the state of balance that is considered safe in maritime, and the targeted situation for all commercial ships is stable equilibrium.
, geminin küçük bir yatma sonrasında yat: is the situation in which the ship's roll angle continues to increase after a small heel. In this case, the position of the center of gravity and the center of lift produces a moment that magnifies the lean. When the ship is moved away from its equilibrium position, it tends to topple further instead of coming back. Such a state of balance is extremely dangerous in practice and can lead to the ship capsizing.
, geminin seyir boyunca stabilitesini do: directly affects the stability of the ship throughout the navigation. A typical consumption sequence is as follows: settling tank and service tank are constantly on for daily use; then the upper fuel tanks are consumed (removing high VCG weights increases GM); then double bottom fuel tanks are used and deep tanks are consumed last. This sequence ensures a controlled decrease in KG and preservation of GM throughout the navigation.
, GM'in en düşük olduğu yükleme konfigür: is the loading configuration with the lowest GM. This condition is usually caused by a combination of the following conditions: high VCG (loading into upper holds or above deck), low KM (low draft or certain trim situations) and maximum free surface effect (large number of partially filled tanks). The situation where GM is minimum may not always be the fully loaded situation; Due to the change in the KM value, especially in partial loading situations, GM may drop to a critical level in an unexpected loading configuration.
, gözlenen cismin ufuk üzerindeki yüksek: , the height of the observed object above the horizon
, güverte üstüne yükleme yapılan gemiler: is a frequently encountered scenario on ships with above-deck loading. Above-deck stowing of 6 to 10 layers high on container ships significantly increases the VCG. On Ro-Ro ships, vehicle decks add weight to the highest points of the ship. In passenger ships, the weight of the superstructures is a factor that keeps the KG high even at the design stage.
, henüz kesinleşmemiş ancak seyri etkile: is published for information that is not yet final but may affect the course. Planned constructions and regulations expected to change in the future are in this group. It is placed on the chart as a warning.
, IMO Balast Su Yönetimi Sözleşmesi (BWM: Within the scope of the IMO Ballast Water Management Convention (BWM Convention), it is an operation that must be carried out in waters more than 200 NM away from the shore and deeper than 200 m. Two methods are applied:
, IMO Tahıl Kodu (International Code for: is subject to special regulations under the IMO Grain Code (International Code for the Safe Carriage of Grain in Bulk). Grain settles over time after loading and creates voids in the cargo hold. When the ship tilts, the grain slides into these gaps and shifts the center of gravity to the tilted side. This shift reduces the righting lever and increases the risk of the ship overturning.
, kalkış ve varış arasındaki geçiş dönem: covers the transition periods between departure and arrival. Fuel consumption at 50%, partial unloading or loading situations, and temporary situations occurring during ballast transfers fall into this category. Intermediate states can be critical for stability, especially during periods when the free surface effect is maximum.
, kargonun iskele veya sancak tarafına d: occurs when the cargo is distributed unevenly to port or starboard. This situation causes initial heel and makes the GZ curve asymmetrical. Unilateral loading is extremely dangerous, especially in low GM situations; because GZ values on the lying side decrease rapidly.
, kendiliğinden tutuşma, metan gazı oluş: , carries additional risks such as auto-ignition, methane gas formation and moisture absorption. The oxidation of coal produces heat, and if ventilation is inadequate the temperature can reach the ignition point. Additionally, methane gas from coal can create explosive mixtures in closed cargo holds. For this reason, regular temperature and gas measurements are mandatory in coal bunkers.
, kesme kuvveti ve eğilme momentinin hiç: requires that the shear force and bending moment do not exceed the permissible limits in any intermediate case. Symmetrical loading is a fundamental requirement of this principle: port and starboard tanks must be filled or emptied simultaneously. Additionally, the weight distribution between bow and stern must be balanced; Excessive local loading should be avoided and weight changes should be spread over the length of the ship as much as possible.
, konteyner gemileri için özellikle tehl: is a particularly dangerous phenomenon for container ships. The large bow and stern flares of modern container ships cause the waterline area to vary greatly during wave passage. This change causes the GM to increase and decrease periodically and under certain wave conditions can create resonance, causing oscillation angles to exceed 40°. Parametric roll is one of the most common causes of container loss, and annually thousands of containers fall overboard due to this phenomenon.
, konteyner gemilerinde özellikle kritik: is particularly critical on container ships. Above-deck container stacks create huge lateral projection area. This field combines with wind pressure to produce a high heeling moment. This field is used directly in IMO Weather Criterion calculations and determines the wind heeling arm value. Each layer of deck stacking increases the wind area and therefore the heeling moment.
, konteyner gemilerinde stabilite yöneti: is a practical tool for stability management on container ships. The basic principles are: heavy containers are placed as low as possible (VCG is reduced); reefer containers are positioned close to energy sources; Containers containing dangerous goods are stowage in accordance with IMDG separation rules and accessibility is planned according to the order of the discharge port.
, konteyner gemilerinin en temel stabili: is the most basic stability problem of container ships. Modern container ships can stack 6 to 10 layers of containers above deck. This stowing significantly raises VCG and lowers GM. Stowage VCG calculation is done as follows:

, stabilitenin en kritik anlara ulaştığı: , are special cases where stability reaches the most critical moments. When the ship enters the dry dock, the weight of the ship begins to be carried by the keel blocks as the water recedes. During the receding process, the buoyancy force of the ship decreases and the keel block reaction force (P) increases. The critical instant is the point at which GM drops to zero and the ship is now balanced on keel blocks without the support of water:
, tam dolu olmayan tanklardaki serbest y: is the period when the free surface effect in tanks that are not fully filled is maximum. Particularly during ballast change, intermediate stages of fuel consumption and partial cargo loading/unloading operations, many tanks may be partially full. In this case, the total FSM value increases rapidly and GMeff may drop to critical levels.
, tank sıralamasının üçüncü kritik boyut: is the third critical dimension of tank ranking. Keeping the number of partially filled tanks as low as possible minimizes total FSM. The practical application of this principle is as follows: one tank should not be moved to the next tank before it is completely filled or completely emptied. Tanks with large widths should be filled or emptied first; because the FSM values of these tanks are very large in proportion to the cube of the width.
, tip onayını almış yazılımın belirli bi: is the verification that type-approved software is customized for a specific ship. At this stage, it is checked that the ship's hydrostatic data, tank capacities and lightship information are entered into the software correctly. Inclining experiment results are integrated and verified that the software produces these ship-specific calculations correctly. Ship-based approval is completed with on-board verification by the classification society surveyor.
, uzun süreli veya kalıcı değişiklikleri: It involves long-term or permanent changes. Adding a new buoy, changing the location or light character of a lighthouse, and adding a new shipwreck to the chart fall into this group. These corrections are on the chart
, yazılımın genel olarak denizcilik stan: is the process that certifies the software's general compliance with maritime standards. The classification society examines the software's algorithms, calculation accuracy and user interface. Test scenarios are applied and the calculation results are compared with known correct values. The permissible calculation deviation is generally limited to ±2%. The type approval documents that the software can be used on all ships; However, its validity alone is not sufficient for a particular ship.
, yerel meridyene göre açısal konumu ise: is the angular position relative to the local meridian
, yükleme bilgisayarı kullanımının en kr: Loading is the most critical phase of computer use. When entering tank data, the sounding or ullage value of each tank is measured and entered into the software. The density (API gravity or direct density value) and temperature of the liquid must also be entered; because temperature correction directly affects the accuracy of the weight calculation, especially in fuel tanks. In the cargo data entry, the weight and stowing position (VCG, LCG coordinates) of each cargo batch are specified. Lightship data and hydrostatic tables are built into the software and are not modified by the user.
, yükleme operasyonlarının ayna görüntüs: Although it may seem like a mirror image of loading operations, it carries additional risks. During unloading, the ship's displacement decreases; Therefore, the KM value changes and GM may decrease unexpectedly. Additionally, adequate propeller immersion must be ensured, minimum draft requirements must be met and trim control must be maintained. Discharging too quickly, unbalanced discharging and delayed ballast removal are the most common hazards.
, yüksek yoğunlukları nedeniyle özel zor: Dense cargoes present particular challenges. Low stowage factor can concentrate a large mass in a small volume. Loading low in the ship can reduce KG and increase GM, producing a stiff response. Check local tank-top loads, hull strength and the complete approved stability criteria; high GM alone does not establish safety.

12’ler kuralı şu varsayımları gerektirir: The rule of 12 requires the following assumptions: (1) the tidal cycle is exactly six hours; (2) The transition between HW and LW follows the symmetrical sinusoidal form. When these conditions are met, the rule gives a reasonable approximation; However, in many ports these conditions are not met.
12’ler kuralı, altı saatlik standart gel: The rule of 12s approximates the rate at which water height changes over the standard six-hour tidal cycle. The tide changes 1/12 of the Range in the first hour; 2/12 in the second hour; 3/12 in the third hour; 3/12 in the fourth hour; 2/12 in the fifth hour; 1/12 in the sixth hour. Total 12/12 = full range, that is, the transition from HW to LW or LW to HW is completed.
12’ler kuralı, LW’den HW’ye veya HW’den:
The rule of 12s is a practical mnemonic rule that gives an approximation of the ratio of the water height change to the total range occurring each hour in a standard six-hour tidal cycle from LW to HW or HW to LW. The basic premise of the rule is that the tidal curve is close to sinusoidal and therefore changes fastest at mid-tide and slowest at the ends (around HW and LW).

Rule: the total range (HW − LW) is divided into 12 equal parts. The change occurring every hour is at the rates of 1/12, 2/12, 3/12, 3/12, 2/12, 1/12, respectively. The sum of these ratios is 12/12 = 1 (full range). The method is extremely practical, especially for fast and visual calculations; It is possible to draw in a notebook or do mental calculations.
12’ler kuralı: gelgit her saatte 1, 2, 3: Rule of 12s: the tide changes by 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1 (in 1/12 of the range) every hour.

2005 Protokolü, SUA'yı klasik gemi kaçır: The 2005 Protocol took SUA beyond the classic ship hijacking scenario and criminalized the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction (WMD) by sea and the use of ships as tools of environmental/nuclear terrorism. The new criminal offenses include using a ship to transport nuclear, chemical or biological weapons or sensitive material or technology used in their production, using a ship as a weapon to cause death or serious injury (for example, crashing into a facility or another ship), and creating a threat of environmental or human harm by deliberately releasing oil, liquefied gas or other hazardous/harmful substances from the ship. This expansion has transformed the SUA from a classic 'ship security' convention into a legal barrier against mass destruction scenarios that can be carried out by sea. Jurisdiction and extradition mechanisms operate with the same 'trial or extradition' logic, but due to the international nature of WMD crimes, requests for interstate intelligence sharing and mutual legal assistance have a higher priority and urgency; When a state detects a suspect under SUA 2005 on its territory, it is obliged to operate expedited procedures to prosecute that person or immediately extradite him to a requesting state. The protocol is also complemented by a parallel protocol (Fixed Platform Protocol) that regulates similar offenses against fixed platforms.

2018 stratejisi ile 2023 revizyonu arası: The main conceptual difference between the 2018 strategy and the 2023 revision is how the target is defined. The 2018 text focused heavily on carbon intensity (emissions per transport) reduction; The shortcoming of this approach was that as the sector grows (more ships, more haulage) total emissions can rise in absolute terms even as density improves – volume growth can more than compensate for this as density falls. By closing this gap, the 2023 revision clearly targets the absolute reduction of 'total annual greenhouse gas emissions' compared to the base year of 2008; This means a real emissions cap, regardless of the growth of the sector. This shift is important because intensity targets alone do not guarantee the sector's total impact on the climate, while absolute targets limit the total amount of carbon released directly into the atmosphere; This explains why medium-term measures (fuel standard, MBM) that will force absolute reductions are added alongside intensity-based instruments such as EEXI/CII.

406 MHz EPIRB, COSPAS-SARSAT uydu sistem: The 406 MHz EPIRB transmits the distress signal via the COSPAS-SARSAT satellite system. The signal includes the ship's identity (MMSI or registration number), GPS position (if equipped with a GPS module) and distress status. COSPAS-SARSAT satellites receive this signal and transmit it to LUT (Local User Terminal) stations, which transmit it to the relevant MRCC (Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre). With GPS-integrated EPIRB, position accuracy drops to approximately 100 m; In models without GPS, location is determined by the Doppler effect, which is slower and less accurate (2–5 km). EPIRB additionally emits a 121.5 MHz homing signal, allowing aircraft and helicopters to be guided at close range.

One of the new generation MEOSAR capabilities is the Return Link Service (RLS): the system can report back to the device that the alarm has been received and processed; so that the person in distress confirms (e.g. by an indicator on the device) that help is on the way; This is valuable for morale and decision-making. Complementary beacons such as AIS-SART and EPIRB-AIS also support close-range positioning at the scene.

ABD'nin denetim sistemi, diğer bölgesel: The US system of control differs fundamentally from other regional regimes: the US is a member of neither the Paris nor the Tokyo MoU; enforces its own independent and often more stringent PSC regime through the USCG (United States Coast Guard). This means that US federal laws as well as international conventions are involved in the audit. Every foreign-flagged ship entering U.S. ports is subject to this regime from the moment it enters territorial waters. This independence makes the United States one of the jurisdictions with the highest bar for maritime compliance.
ABD'ye giren gemiler, uluslararası sözle: Ships entering the United States must meet a number of additional requirements specific to US federal legislation as well as international conventions. EPA's Vessel General Permit (VGP) regulates ship-related discharges; The USA's own ballast water rules require a USCG type approved BWMS (IMO approval alone is not sufficient). The USCG publishes policy and practice guidelines through NVICs (Navigation and Vessel Inspection Circulars), which are regularly updated; NVIC monitoring is critical for issues such as cybersecurity, BWM and environmental compliance. Electronic notification of arrival (eNOA) is required within 96 hours prior to entry. The Master of the Port (COTP) has broad powers to stop ship movements in his area, declare safety zones and issue special orders; this makes the US regime more centralized and direct than other MoUs.

AFS Sözleşmesi, ilk bakışta teknik bir a: The AFS Convention regulates ship underwater paints, which at first glance seem like a technical detail but are a serious environmental problem. Anti-fouling paints are used to prevent marine creatures (mussels, algae, crustaceans) from adhering to the hull of ships; These paints reduce friction and save fuel. However, TBT (tributyltin) compounds, which were widely used in the past, leaked into the water and caused damage far beyond the target: gender distortions in sea snails, deformations in oyster shells, and widespread destruction in the ecosystem. By banning these harmful biocides, AFS aims to separate the benefit of the dye from its environmental cost.
AFS survey gereklilikleri ve sertifika d: AFS establishes survey requirements and certification issuance procedures.
AFS uyumu belge düzeyinde de izlenir. 40: AFS compliance is also monitored at the document level. International expedition ships of 400 GT and above must carry the International Anti-fouling System Certificate (AFS Certificate), while smaller ships must carry the AFS Declaration; These documents indicate the type of paint used, application date and compatibility. When the paint is changed or during the dry-dock period, a survey is carried out and the certificate is updated. No international voyages can be made without a certificate or declaration; If a prohibited substance or document incompatibility is detected during the PSC inspection, there is a risk of deficiency registration and detention. Thus, AFS turns an environmental prohibition into an auditable compliance obligation.
AFS uyumunun kanıtlanabilmesi, boyanın f: The ability to prove AFS compliance is closely tied to the moment when the paint is actually applied or replaced; A ship cannot be certified as 'AFS compliant' on an arbitrary date because the only objective evidence of compliance is a physical survey of what anti-fouling system is applied to the hull at that time. The AFS survey is therefore an event with its own logic, independent of the ship's periodic survey schedule: the survey is carried out either at the initial construction of the ship or when the underwater paint is replaced/renewed, so in practice it is locked into the dry-dock period. The operational implication of this is that a shipowner must synchronize the decision to remove old paint containing cybutryne or apply sealant with a dry-dock window when the ship will be dry docked anyway; Otherwise, either true harmony will not be achieved because the paint is not changed, or an unscheduled dry-dock visit will create additional costs and operational interruptions. This dependency makes it necessary for fleet managers to match AFS transition deadlines (e.g. 2026 for cybutryne) early with each ship's own dry-dock planning.

Heavy weather navigation is a special navigation regime in which certain speed, route and operation decisions are made in order to protect the structural integrity, stability and crew safety of the ship in strong wind and wave conditions. The fundamental principle of this regime is that ship safety is always the first priority, despite ETA or commercial calendar pressure.

Heavy weather navigation is not a purely reactive approach; It is an ambitious foresight and decision process. Before entering a heavy weather zone, a good navigator interprets meteorological data, evaluates route alternatives, and determines the speed-route combination that will manage heavy weather with the least risk.

Dynamic data comes automatically from sensors: position, speed over land (SOG), course over land (COG), heading (rot), rate of turn (ROT) and navigational status — cruising, at anchor, out of command, etc. Voyage data are entered manually at the beginning of each voyage: draft, dangerous cargo status, destination, estimated time of arrival (ETA) and number of people on board. The meaning for the sailor is two-fold: there is very strong wind at high altitudes, and strong rushing winds (katabatic/wave-induced gust, rotor turbulence) should be expected in the lee of mountainous coasts. It generally indicates an unstable middle atmosphere and may indicate weather change within 24–48 hours. APCIS'in gerçek değeri, bir denetçinin g: The real value of APCIS is revealed in an inspector's preliminary inspection before boarding the ship. Without going to the port dock, the inspector sees the ship's region-wide history through APCIS: which member ports it was inspected at, what deficiencies were detected, detention records, if any, and whether they were closed. This means that the inspection is not an isolated event of a single port but is part of a regional continuum: a deficiency identified and uncorked during an inspection in Vietnam, for example, is still visible on the inspector's screen when the ship calls in Australia a month later, directly shaping the scope of that inspection. By the same logic, a detention order obtained in a member port tags the ship not only in that port but in the entire region with access to APCIS; the ship is deemed higher risk at the next port and is more likely to be subject to more thorough inspection. In this regard, APCIS functions as a memory layer that links individual controls and prevents substandard operations from being geographically forgotten; A bad record gained in one port is carried with the ship to all parts of the region.

Appraisal is the first and fundamental stage of the passage planning process within the framework of IMO A.893(21). At this stage, all information specific to the navigation is systematically collected, its updates are checked and it forms the basis for the planning phase. A passage plan prepared without appraisal means that it is built with incomplete or incorrect assumptions and jeopardizes safety.

aşamasında stabilite kaybının başladığın: at this stage, symptoms indicating the beginning of loss of stability should be recognized. A significant lengthening of the rolling period indicates that GM has decreased. If the ship tends to roll to one side from an upright position (loll state), this indicates that the GM is approaching zero or has gone negative. The constantly increasing heel angle and the ship's inability to right itself indicate the beginning of a loss of critical stability.
aşamasında şu eylemler gerçekleştirilir:: in this phase, the following actions are performed: MAYDAY message preparation is made (it is not sent yet, but preparation begins); the machine is ordered to reduce speed or stop; the ship is kept in the safest position against the waves if possible (side wave conditions are avoided); The crew is warned and lifesaving equipment is made ready. Making quick decisions at this stage is critical; However, wrong decisions taken in panic can worsen the situation.
aşamasında, beklenen hava koşulları, yol: at this stage, expected weather conditions, travel time and special conditions on the route (narrow water crossing, shallow water) are taken into account. Basınç gradyanı, birim mesafe başına bas: Pressure gradient is the change in pressure per unit distance. The shorter the distance between two isobars on the synoptic chart, the larger the gradient and therefore the higher the wind speed. The geostrophic wind equation describes this relationship mathematically: wind speed is obtained from the balance of the gradient force and the Coriolis force. However, due to surface friction, the real wind blows approximately 20–30% slower than the geostrophic wind and with a deviation of 15°–30° towards the high pressure side of the isobars. Since the friction on the sea is less than on land, the wind moves closer to the geostrophic value.

This section; It details sampling discipline, analysis parameters, trend interpretation, condition-based oil change decision and PMS integration.

This responsibility; It covers performance monitoring, condition monitoring, fuel management, MARPOL compliance, class survey preparation and critical failure decision making. This chapter covers in detail the day-to-day management of a modern 2-stroke low-speed diesel main engine, its performance indicators, common malfunctions and the Chief Engineer's decision matrix.
Baş Mühendis (Chief Engineer), geminin s: The Chief Engineer is responsible for the final preparation of the ship's mechanical department for class and flag state surveys. It systematically manages annual, intermediate and special survey cycles, Continuous Machinery Survey (CMS) program, condition of class notes and PSC/vetting inspections. This section; It covers in detail survey schedule management, use of PMS as survey evidence, test/trial planning and common findings in audits.
Baş Mühendis (Chief Engineer), geminin t: The Chief Engineer is the critical communication link that conveys the technical status of the ship to the onshore management in a transparent, timely and data-based manner. All technical reporting, from daily noon report to monthly technical report, from malfunction notification to repair/maintenance coordination, is the responsibility of the Chief Engineer. This section; It discusses in detail the reporting hierarchy, fuel/oil consumption reporting, noon report data, defect reporting and effective communication with Superintendent.

The Chief Engineer is responsible for managing the maintenance schedule of all machinery and auxiliary equipment of the ship through the Planned Maintenance System (PMS). This responsibility; It includes opening and approving work orders, checking the accuracy of records, confirming that maintenance is actually carried out not only on the software but also in the field, and monitoring maintenance performance with KPIs. PMS records are the primary evidence document in classification (CMS) and flag state surveys; Incomplete or false registration will result in detention of the vessel and suspension of class conditions. This chapter details the installation, control and continuous improvement of PMS on a modern ship.
Baş Mühendis (Chief Engineer), makine da: The Chief Engineer is the technical decision maker and response coordinator for ship safety in emergency situations originating from the engine room. Makes fast, accurate and calm decisions in scenarios such as black-out recovery, main engine failure, emergency steering, engine room fire and flooding; Manages the machine team in drill and real intervention. This section; It discusses in detail the main emergency scenarios, response procedures, decision matrix, drill discipline and coordination with the bridge.
Baş Mühendis (Chief Engineer), makine de: Chief Engineer is the highest manager of the mechanical department. Responsible for the operational integrity of all technical systems including main engine, auxiliary engines, generators, boiler, cooling systems, ballast/billion pumps, fuel/oil systems, shaft and propeller. It is the ultimate guarantor of the safe operation of the machinery department under the ISM Code. He is of equivalent seniority to the Master and has the authority to make independent decisions on technical matters.

The Chief Engineer determines the operational success of the mechanical department not only through technical knowledge; It ensures correct task distribution, watch discipline, competence development and a strong safety culture. Manages STCW qualifications, familiarization processes and continuous training of the entire team, from the Second Engineer to the machine crew. This section; It discusses in detail the role and responsibility matrix, watchkeeping scheme, competency assessment, vendor-specific and safety trainings and human element management from the perspective of the Chief Engineer.
Baş Mühendis (Chief Engineer), MARPOL An: The Chief Engineer is the technical responsible for the ship's EEXI (Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index), CII (Carbon Intensity Indicator) and SEEMP Part III compliance within the scope of MARPOL Annex VI Chapter 4. Conducts technical evaluation of speed and trim optimization, hull/propeller cleaning, waste heat recovery and alternative fuel options; Manages the maintenance of the CII rating and the preparation of a corrective action plan when necessary. This section; It discusses in detail the carbon intensity regime, EEXI/CII calculation, energy efficiency measures and adaptation strategies.

Chief Engineer is the technical designer and supervisor of the fuel changeover process at the entrances and exits to ECA (Emission Control Area) areas in accordance with MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 14. Timing of the changeover, purging time calculation, viscosity and temperature control and changeover logbook discipline are critical for both compliance and machine safety. This section; It discusses the sulfur regime, changeover procedure, purging calculation, equipment risks and PSC inspection in detail.
Baş Mühendis (Chief Engineer), şaft hatt: The Chief Engineer is responsible for the health of the shaft line and especially the stern tube system. Stern tube bearing lubrication, aft/fore seal sealing, oil sampling program, propeller boss cap injection monitoring, shaft alignment and weardown measurement are critical items. Stern tube oil spill is marine pollution within the scope of MARPOL Annex I. This section; It covers stern tube types, seal management, oil analysis, weardown monitoring, vibration monitoring and MARPOL dimension in detail.

Bir gemi ECA sınırına yaklaştığında yüks: When a ship approaches the ECA limit, it cannot instantaneously switch from high sulfur fuel to low sulfur fuel; Changeover is a procedure that must be carefully planned due to the difference in viscosity and density between fuel types. Since HSFO is typically high viscosity, it is transported by heating in the fuel line and in the machine; Low sulfur distillate fuels such as MGO have much lower viscosity and if pumped at the same temperature can cause wear in fuel pumps due to insufficient lubrication. Therefore, the changeover is initiated sufficiently before the ECA limit is reached (usually hours before, depending on distance and machine type); The fuel temperature is gradually reduced, the system is monitored until the fuel lines and filters are completely purged of old fuel, and the risk of intermediate product formation and clogging is monitored until the transition is completed. The flag state is obliged to ensure compliance of ships flying its flag with international conventions (SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, MLC), register, certify and inspect them. Bir gemi seyir halindeyken gövdesinin su: While a ship is underway, the submerged part of its hull (hull plates, propeller, rudder, sea connections) cannot be seen and inspected; However, these areas are the places most exposed to corrosion, biological contamination and mechanical wear. A dry dock inspection opens this unseen half to physical inspection by docking the ship and draining the water. SOLAS and classification rules require this inspection: typically two dry dock inspections are carried out within the five-year certification cycle, and the interval between inspections cannot exceed 36 months. For ships that meet certain conditions, underwater inspection (IWS) by diver or ROV may be an alternative.

Bir gemi yıllık limitin üzerinde kalırsa: If a ship remains above the annual limit, the resulting deficit is monetized with a fixed penalty rate based on the VLSFO equivalent amount of energy, and this penalty is not a one-off; If the deficit is not paid, the debt is carried forward to the next year with interest, and a deficit for two consecutive years makes the penalty even heavier. This cost structure explains why pooling within the fleet is often cheaper than paying the penalty directly: a sister ship running on clean fuel (e.g. high percentages of biofuel or methanol) remains well below standard, producing a large surplus; Transferring this surplus to the deficit ship through a commercial agreement may provide compensation for less than the full amount of the penalty, because the pooling price is freely negotiable between the parties and the market penalty acts as a ceiling price. As a result, the right question for the fleet manager is not 'does this ship meet the limit on its own', but 'does the total energy portfolio of the fleet meet the limit and how can the excess be distributed most efficiently?'

Bir gemide ECDIS, enfekte bir USB ile ya: On one ship, ECDIS behaved abnormally after a chart update via an infected USB. Investigation showed that the media was infected on a land computer. Lesson: all portable media should be scanned at a separate scanning kiosk before use.

Bir gemide farklı supplier'lardan alınan: On one ship, two distillates from different suppliers were mixed in transit; Asphaltene-like precipitation clogged the filters and the main engine lost power in the ECA approach. Bir gemide gece zabiti, generator'da yük: On one ship, the night officer did not report or intervene about the rising bearing temperature in the generator "in order not to disturb the Chief Engineer at this hour"; In the morning the bearing was damaged. Bir gemide GRB'ye gerçekte denize atılan: On one ship, waste that was actually thrown into the sea was recorded on the GRB as "delivered"; It was noticed at the PSC that there was no delivery receipt and intentional violation proceedings were initiated. Bir gemide hasta mürettebatın çamaşırını: On a ship, the infection spread to more than one person as a result of the sick crew's laundry not being processed separately. Bir gemide header tank seviyesinin hafta: A weekly decreasing trend of the header tank level on a ship and an increase in water in the oil analysis indicated early aft seal lip wear. Bir geminin dönüş davranışı birkaç temel: The turning behavior of a ship is defined by several basic parameters. Advance: the distance traveled in the direction of the original course from the moment the turn order is given until the ship turns 90° from the new heading. Transfer: the distance crossed transverse to the original route line in the same stage. Tactical Diameter: Transverse distance from the original heading line when the 180° turn is completed – this value often determines the critical aerodrome requirement for the turn.

This chapter explains in concrete ways the discipline of spare parts and calibration in an environment where maritime supply delays are high.

Bir geminin trafik deseni değiştiğinde (: When a ship's traffic pattern changes (for example, when a ship operating in coastal waters moves to open ocean voyages), the sea area in which it is certified must also be upgraded, and this requires the actual installation of additional equipment on the ship, not a paper update. While a ship certified only in A1 can be satisfied with VHF DSC, moving to A2 requires the addition of an MF DSC transmitter, moving to A3 requires the installation of an Inmarsat terminal or HF equipment, and moving to A4 requiring HF DSC. If a ship sails outside the sea area for which it has been certified without installing the necessary equipment, this is both a direct violation of SOLAS Chapter IV and an actual safety gap: the ship does not have the system to transmit the distress call in that area. PSC and flag state inspections compare the ship's actual sailing area (final ports, planned route) with the sea area declaration on the certificate; If a non-compliance is detected, this is a direct deficiency and, in serious cases, a reason for detention. Therefore, before a ship's commercial zone is expanded, upgrading its radio equipment and updating the certificate accordingly is a prerequisite for operational planning.

Bir sörveyör standart altı bir durum bul: When a surveyor finds substandard condition, the tools available to the class are gradual. At the lightest end is the 'recommendation', which is not required but is noted. More serious findings are recorded as 'Condition of Class' (CoC) and require closure within a certain period of time (usually several months, sometimes until the next port); During this period the ship remains in class but is under surveillance. If time is exceeded and correction is not made, the class is suspended — this is a formal determination that the ship no longer complies with the class requirements and is usually reversible. The most severe consequence is the complete withdrawal of the class (withdrawal); This is not just a suspension, it is the classification society's termination of its relationship with the ship, and re-entering the class requires an evaluation from scratch. The practical consequences of Withdrawal are quickly chained: as P&I clubs and car insurers often make their policies conditional on 'being in class', loss of class means a virtual end to insurance cover; In the event of an accident or pollution incident, the insurer may refuse to pay. Since flag state certificates are mostly based on class approval, withdrawal causes these certificates to be suspended and the ship to become unnavigable.

This responsibility; It covers cargo plan preparation, stability and trim calculations, tank/hold preparation, lashing/securing control, IMO class dangerous cargo procedures, ballast management, terminal coordination and accuracy of cargo documents. This section explains step by step the methodology that the Chief Officer should follow in daily load management.

Birinci Zabit, çoğu gemide ISM kapsamınd: The Chief Officer is the Safety Officer appointed under ISM on most ships. This role; Organizing safety committee meetings, collecting and analyzing near-miss and safety observation cards, following corrective/preventive actions (CAPA), executing the drill program and preparing a response to internal audit findings and reporting them to the company DPA. This section explains how the ISM Code is reflected in the field and how safety culture is measured and improved.
Birinci Zabit, gemideki tüm LSA (Life-Sa: The Chief Officer is ultimately responsible for inventory control, maintenance tracking, tracking service dates and keeping records of all LSA (Life-Saving Appliances) and FFE (Fire-Fighting Equipment) equipment on board. Although the actual execution is often delegated to the Third Officer, liferafts, lifeboats, life jackets, fire extinguishing systems, muster list updates and drill organization are under the coordination of the Chief Officer. This chapter systematically addresses safety equipment management within the framework of the SOLAS and LSA/FSS Code.
Birinci Zabit, gemideki yüksek riskli iş: The Chief Officer is directly responsible for controlling high-risk work on the ship with the Permit to Work (PTW) system. Enclosed space entry, hot work, working aloft, working overside and electrical/insulation works; It cannot be started without risk assessment, toolbox meeting, isolation (LOTO), atmosphere testing and field supervision. This chapter explains step by step the setup of the permit system, risk assessment methodology, PPE compliance and field inspection practice within the framework of ISM/SOLAS.
Birinci Zabit, geminin her yükleme/boşal: The Chief Officer is the person who ensures that the ship remains within adequate intact stability and hull strength at each loading/unloading stage and throughout the entire voyage. Keeping GM, trim, bending moment and shear force values within approved stability booklet and loading manual limits; Planning ballast operations within the framework of BWMP and managing hazards such as free surface, list and parametric rolling are the essence of this task. This chapter explains the Chief Officer's methodology from the theory of stability calculation to field application.
Birinci Zabit, geminin ticari operasyonu: The Chief Officer is the person who prepares and signs critical documents in the commercial operation of the ship. Notice of Readiness (NOR) is the official notification to the charterer or terminal operator that the ship is ready for loading/unloading; The timing directly affects the laytime and demurrage calculation within the scope of the charter party. Statement of Facts (SoF) records the entire port operation; Mate's Receipt confirms the cargo quantity and apparent status; Letter of Protest is issued for suspicious cargo. An error in these documents could cost the company tens of thousands of dollars. This section describes the Chief Officer's business/legal document management.
Birinci Zabit, güverte departmanı açısın: The Chief Officer is primarily responsible for the environmental compatibility of the ship in terms of the deck department. This responsibility; Implementation of the Garbage Management Plan includes control of sludge operations, operational preparation of SOPEP (Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan) procedures and prevention of pollution risks in deck areas. Incidents of marine pollution can result in high fines, ship arrest and even imprisonment; US MARPOL violations are notorious for millions of bollard in fines. This section describes the Chief Officer's MARPOL compliant environmental management methodology.

The Chief Officer is responsible for the preparation of PSC (Port State Control), vetting, flag state and class inspections for the deck department. This responsibility; It includes keeping safety equipment records, PMS logs, drill records, risk assessment archives and work permit files in accordance with the audit format. A detention keeps the ship in the port for days, causing the company to lose reputation and money; A vetting failure may result in loss of charter. This section explains how the Chief Officer establishes an inspection-ready ship culture.
Birinci Zabit, güverte departmanının (de: The Chief Officer is the direct superior of the deck department and the orchestrator of daily business life. This section; It deals in detail with the management methodology that the Chief Officer should follow regarding watch patterns, work planning, new staff orientation, performance monitoring and staff welfare.
Birinci Zabit, güverte departmanının ope: The Chief Officer is the operational chief of the deck department. He is credited with the role of "loadmaster"; He/she is actually responsible for loading/unloading planning, stability calculations, deck maintenance and safety equipment. Within the scope of the ISM Code, he usually serves as a Safety Officer and on most ships he also serves as an SSO (Ship Security Officer). As the most senior deck officer on the ship after the Master, he assumes command of the ship in the Master's absence.
Birinci Zabit, güverte departmanının Pla: The Chief Officer is the planner and supervisor of all maintenance activities within the deck department's Planned Maintenance System (PMS). Preparing the maintenance schedule for cranes, mooring winches, hatch covers, ropes and wires, paint system and deck machinery, distributing work orders, coordinating with material/parts procurement and recording completion is the essence of this task. PMS discipline is also a measure of the Chief Officer's reputation as delay in maintenance is a direct finding in the class/PSC inspection. This responsibility includes preparing the mooring plan, rigging the rope and wire layout correctly, identifying snap-back zones and positioning personnel safely. Mooring operations have some of the highest injury and fatality rates in shipping; this section explains, step by step, the method the Chief Officer must follow to keep the manoeuvre safe.

Black Sea MoU kuruldu – Karadeniz kıyı d: Black Sea MoU established – PSC coordination between Black Sea coastal states begins
Black Sea MoU, Karadeniz'e kıyısı olan a: The Black Sea MoU coordinates port state control of six Black Sea littoral countries (Bulgaria, Georgia, Romania, Russia, Turkey, Ukraine). The region has an interesting structural feature: Bulgaria and Romania, which are EU members, are also members of the Paris MoU, while Türkiye is included in both the Black Sea and Mediterranean MoU. These overlapping memberships ensure that Black Sea inspections are carried out in close compliance with the Paris MoU standards. Audit data is shared through the BS-INFO regional system and appears common among members.
Black Sea MoU, yalnızca altı üye devletl: The Black Sea MoU is a small bloc compared to the Paris or Tokyo MoU, with only six member states; However, this smallness does not reduce the value of data sharing, on the contrary, it makes it more manageable and focused. Inspection results, deficiencies and detention records shared through the BS-INFO system prevent significant duplication even in a region with a limited number of ports: once a ship is inspected in Constanta and a deficiency is detected, this information also becomes visible to the next inspector in Odessa or Novorossiysk and the focus can be on following up on those previously detected rather than unnecessary re-inspection. The small membership size also speeds up coordination: determination of CIC campaign themes and joint implementation decisions go through fewer bureaucratic layers than with multi-member MoUs. The dual membership of Bulgaria and Romania in the Paris MoU ensures that BS-INFO remains in indirect alignment with THETIS; In this way, even a small regional system contributes to the data integrity of the larger European PSC network.
Black Sea MoU'nun en belirleyici yapısal: The most defining structural feature of the Black Sea MoU is that some of its members are also included in the Paris MoU: EU members Bulgaria and Romania are subject to both the Black Sea and Paris regimes and carry out supervision under the EU PSC Directive (2009/16/EC). This dual membership ensures that Black Sea inspections are carried out in close compliance with the Paris MoU standards and the THETIS data infrastructure; Risk profile calculation, deficiency coding, and detention criteria are largely common. Türkiye is a member of both the Black Sea and Mediterranean MoU and is one of the countries that manages the busiest maritime traffic in the region. These overlapping memberships make the Black Sea not an isolated region but part of the broader Euro-Mediterranean PSC network.

BRM’de karar alma, tek kişinin sezgisine: Decision making in BRM is based on structured processes, not a single person's intuition. Especially in maneuver decisions, the FORDEC model (Facts, Options, Risks/benefits, Decision, Execution, Check) or similar structured frameworks are used. The culture of team members 'not being afraid to ask questions' ensures that errors are caught early. In error management, the 'trap-error-consequence' model (Threat and Error Management, TEM) is adopted: first the threat is detected, and if the error is not prevented before it occurs, the result of the error is managed. In BRM training, simulator scenarios are used to evaluate the communication quality and decision processes of the teams under pressure. Part A-VIII of the STCW defines the legal framework for bridge watchkeeping standards, use of navigation equipment and safe ship management.
BRM’nin çekirdeğinde üç temel bileşen bu: At the core of BRM are three key components: leadership and authority management, clear communication and continuous situational awareness. In terms of leadership, the Master is the person who directs the bridge team and makes the final decision; But an effective leader actively solicits subordinate opinions and does not allow the authority gradient (authority difference) to grow excessively. Excessive authority gradients cause subordinate personnel to fail to convey critical information, predisposing to accidents. Standard terminology and the closed-loop verification (read-back/hear-back) principle are essential in communication: every instruction given must be repeated and confirmed. Situational awareness is when the team shares a common mental model about ship location, traffic, meteorology and passage plan; When this pattern is disrupted, 'loss of situational awareness' occurs and is the most common precursor to major accidents.

A common strategy to address this uncertainty is to choose a dual-fuel or 'fuel-ready' design rather than sticking to a single fuel: the ship is built to run on a fuel that is available and economical today (e.g. LNG or conventional fuel + high biofuel blend capacity), but the engine room, fuel tanks and pipeline layout are designed so that it can be converted to methanol or ammonia at relatively low cost in the future. The cost of this approach is a higher initial investment than for a pure mono-fuel ship, but the trade-off is the ability to adapt over the economic life of the ship, regardless of which mid-term measure (levy, ETS, fuel standard) prevails. Shipowners also complement this hedging strategy by adding regulatory change clauses to charter contracts and monitoring infrastructure investments in the fuel supply chain (port bunkering capacity).

Rising air cools adiabatically; Condensation begins when the temperature reaches the dew point, and this level determines the cloud base. There are four basic mechanisms that raise the air: convection (heating from the bottom by the sun or the warm sea surface), orographic uplift (the air hitting the mountain or high coastline and climbing), frontal uplift (the rise of warm air over the cold mass) and convergence (the upward forcing of air currents that meet at the surface). Which mechanism is active also determines the type of cloud that will be formed: convection produces cluster (cumulus) clouds, while large-area slow rise produces stratiform clouds.

BWM Sözleşmesi iki standart tanımlar ve: The BWM Convention defines two standards and the industry has moved from one to the other. D-1 (ballast water exchange) envisages replacing at least 95% of the ballast volume offshore (or pumping three times the volume); This is done at least 200 miles offshore and at a depth of 200 metres. D-1 is a temporary and partial solution: the replacement is not always fully effective, depends on weather conditions and can challenge the structural safety of the ship. D-2 (performance standard) is the permanent solution and reduces the density of living organisms in the discharged water to very low numerical limits: no more than 10 per cubic meter of organisms ≥50 microns in size, no more than 10 per milliliter of organisms between 10-50 microns, and separate limits for certain indicator bacteria (toxigenic cholera, E. coli, enterococci). A treatment system (BWMS) that provides this is installed on the ship.
BWM Sözleşmesi, gemilerin denge için ald: The BWM Convention manages the environmental threat posed by organisms that ships carry from one sea to another with the ballast water they take for balance. Species that are harmless in one area can explode when moved to another ecosystem with no natural enemies, destroying native life, fisheries and infrastructure; Even pathogens such as cholera can be spread this way. The solution of the contract is the obligation to either change the ballast water in the open sea before discharge (D-1) or to treat it in a way that will kill/remove the living creatures in it (D-2). The convention, adopted in 2004, entered into force only after reaching sufficient approval in 2017.

Each deballasting and discharge operation must be fully recorded in the Ballast Water Record Book (BWRB), indicating volume, location, date/time and method used (D-1 exchange or D-2 treatment); these records are one of the first documents reviewed in a PSC inspection, and a deficiency can lead directly to a deficiency code or detention. Frequency of filter backwashing and periodic cleaning of sediment accumulated at tank bottoms both maintains system performance and meets the sediment management obligation defined in the Ballast Water Management Plan (BWMP). UV lamps have a limited lifespan and regular replacement and sensor calibration is essential, as reduced beam power can lead to inadequate disinfection in ports with high water turbidity. If the system fails mid-navigation, the ship enters an adaptation crisis that the crew cannot resolve on their own: the contract provides for 'alternative management practice' (Ballast Water Exchange as contingency) and immediate reporting of the incident to the flag state and port of destination authority; Discharges without repeated fault records are considered as a serious non-compliance in the audit.

BWMS'ler tipik olarak iki aşamalı çalışı: BWMSs typically operate in two stages: first a filter separates large particles and organisms, then a disinfection step such as UV irradiation or electrochlorination inactivates any remaining organisms. The system must carry IMO type approval, be verified by commissioning testing after installation and monitored with annual surveys. For crews, this means recording each ballast operation in the Ballast Water Logbook, timely replacement of UV lamps and filters, calibrating sensors and sediment management. If the system fails, alternative compliance methods and reporting procedures come into play.

Inflatable liferafts are shipped to a flag state-approved service station at the period specified by the manufacturer (usually annually, with extended intervals in some new designs); Here the raft is opened, its tightness, inflation mechanism, hydrostatic release device and emergency supplies inside (water, food, signaling equipment) are checked and replaced one by one. Movement speed is calculated using the time between two charts (usually 6 or 12 hours) and the distance traveled by the front. Cold fronts generally move at a speed of 25–40 knots, and warm fronts at 15–25 knots; however, these values can vary widely. The direction of movement of the front is determined by the pressure direction of the air mass behind it and the upper level flows.

The weakening or strengthening of the front can be observed from the chart series: increasing isobar compression indicates strengthening, relaxation indicates weakening. As the front enters occlusion, the surface effect becomes complex and often begins to weaken.

Minimum rest hours are strict: at least 10 hours of rest in any 24-hour period and at least 77 hours of rest in any 7-day period; The rest can be divided into two parts at most and one part should be at least 6 hours. The principle of 'fitness for duty' also includes alcohol and drug policy; STCW imposes a standard maximum blood alcohol limit (0.05% BAC or 0.25 mg/L breath) on watchstanders. XI-1 includes measures to strengthen maritime safety: the IMO number (identification) of the ship, which does not change throughout its life, the Continuous Synopsis Record (CSR) showing the ship-flag-class history, the mandatory Enhanced Survey Program (ESP) for tankers and bulk carriers, and the requirements for the authorization of classification societies. XI-2 regulates security by requiring the ISPS Code: ship security assessment (SSA), ship security plan (SSP), designated responsible persons (SSO, CSO, PFSO), secret security alarm system (SSAS) and three-tiered security level system. Damage stability and structural strength criteria are defined for ships over 150 m: it is expected that the ship will not sink even if the forwardmost hold receives water, and the bulkheads and double-wall structures are expected to be able to carry this load. Because AER uses the design carrying capacity as the capacity and not the cargo actually carried, it 'penalises' ships sailing empty or half-full, and this is one of the controversial aspects of the methodology. For some types, such as passenger and ro-ro ships, alternative metrics (cgDIST, clDIST) based on gross tonnage or passengers/distance are used. Since the data entering the calculation is collected under the IMO DCS, the CII is a direct output of the DCS; For some special situations such as rescue, ice navigation or STS, voyage adjustments may be deducted from the emissions.

The CII's enforcement is not merely regulatory but strongly commercial: charterers avoid low-grade vessels, reducing freight revenue and the resale value of the vessel; financing and insurance terms may also be affected by rating; GHG assessments from platforms like RightShip reinforce this pressure. Cirrocumulus, gölgesiz küçük beyaz tanel: Cirrocumulus are small white grains without shadows or high clumps arranged in ripples; It is known as 'mackerel sky' in maritime because its appearance resembles fish scales. It is a sign of high levels of turbulence and increased humidity; It is usually seen together with cirrus and cirrostratus and is a harbinger of the approaching frontal system. The saying 'Mackerel sky and mares' tails make lofty ships carry low sails' summarizes for centuries that this cloud indicates bad weather within 24-48 hours. Since it is a short-lived cloud, it should be recorded when seen and the trend should be monitored.
Cirrostratus örtüsüne; tipik olarak 12–3: Cirrostratus cover; weather to break down typically within 12–36 hours
Cirrostratus, gökyüzünü süt beyazı ince: Cirrostratus is a blanket of ice crystals that covers the sky like a thin, milky white veil. Its most distinctive feature is that it creates a 22-degree halo around the sun or moon; Light refracts through hexagonal ice crystals, producing this ring. The appearance of a halo is a classic sign of bad weather: the cirrostratus cover typically extends 500–1000 km ahead of the warm front and heralds the arrival of altostratus followed by nimbostratus precipitation, usually within 12–36 hours. The saying 'a solar halo is a harbinger of a storm' is based on this mechanism. If the cirrostratus thickens and descends, the front is approaching; should be verified along with the barometer trend.
Cirrus, gökyüzünde ince beyaz tüyler, sa: Cirrus is an ice crystal cloud that appears in the sky as thin white feathers, fringes or horsetails. Strong winds (jet streams) in the upper atmosphere drag the crystals, giving them the characteristic hook shape (cirrus uncinus, 'mares' tails'). Scattered and sparse cirrus alone is a sign of good weather; However, cirrus that regularly multiplies, thickens and begins to cover the sky from the western horizon indicates the approach of a warm front or low pressure system within 24–48 hours. The direction of movement of cirrus stripes is used to predict the upper atmospheric flow and hence the direction of arrival of the approaching system.

Close-up survey'in 'yakın' olması lafta: The 'close' nature of a close-up survey is not just a word; The surveyor must actually physically reach a structural member, within arm's reach or hammering distance. This requires staging within the tank or floating on the ballast water with a raft, and setting up these devices can take days in itself. A more fundamental obstacle is making the space safe for human entry: closed tanks are pre-ventilated, the atmosphere is measured for oxygen and toxic/flammable gas, and no personnel can enter without being certified gas-free; This process may take a long time depending on the size of the tank and previous cargo. Preparing and inspecting dozens of holds and ballast tanks sequentially in this way on a large bulk carrier means that the ship is withdrawn from commercial voyages for days, sometimes weeks. That's why shipowners often combine ESP surveys with an already planned dry dock or maintenance stop; Doing it separately increases both cost and lost time.

COLREG (Convention on the International: COLREG (Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972) is an international convention prepared within IMO and entered into force in 1977 to prevent collisions, which are the most destructive type of maritime accidents. COLREG, consisting of 38 rules and annexes, is valid in all waters, including offshore and harbor entrance channels; Without prejudice to the jurisdiction of countries that have rules specific to inland water only. The rules are built on three pillars: constant and effective lookout (Rule 5), safe speed determined by the conditions (Rule 6) and the risk of collision identified and managed at an early stage (Rules 7–8). All these technical rules are complemented by the 'good maritime practice' general provision of Rule 2: if strict adherence to the rules in unusual circumstances creates danger, the Master may take the initiative. For maritime students, COLREG is the basic legal framework that governs daily situations in both examination and real sea life.

The marine equivalent of lanes and traffic lights on the highway; navigation lights, shapes, sound signals and maneuver rules. The basic principle of the convention is that every sailor should be able to put maritime custom and common sense ahead of the rules: Rule 2 states that the rules can never be applied so rigidly as to lead to a collision, and that even departures from the rules when necessary are legitimate to prevent collision. Section B's maneuverability hierarchy is critical: ships restricted in manoeuvrability (RAM), vessels restricted in shallow water (CBD), fishing vessels, sailing vessels and motor ships are ranked, with the motor ship at the bottom of the hierarchy. Knowing this hierarchy is a prerequisite for correctly determining who has the obligation to give way.
COLREG'in giriş bölümü, kuralların nasıl: The preamble of COLREG sets out how the rules are to be interpreted. Rule 1 outlines its scope of application: the high seas and all waters connected thereto in which marine vessels navigate. Rule 2 (liability) is the soul of the contract: no rule exempts the ship, master or crew from the consequences of neglecting the rules; Moreover, when special circumstances require it (imminent danger, narrow water, restricted maneuvering) it is even legitimate to deviate from the rules to avoid a collision. This transforms COLREG from a list to be blindly memorized into a maritime discipline based on situational assessment. Rule 3 defines the terms used throughout the contract (power-propelled ship, sailboat, ship with limited manoeuvrability, ship not under command, sight of each other, restricted view); These definitions are key to the correct application of subsequent rules.

Crossing (kesişme) durumu, COLREG'in en: The crossing situation is one of the most frequently encountered and also one of the most misinterpreted scenarios of COLREG. If two motor ships are cutting each other's route at the same time in a way that creates a risk of collision and this situation does not fall within the scope of head-on or overtaking, Rule 15 comes into play. Crossing figures prominently in maritime accident statistics worldwide: incorrect ship assignment (which is the 'give-way'), late or inadequate maneuvering and miscommunication over VHF are major sources of error. For maritime faculty students, understanding the crossing scenario with its geometric, legal and operational dimensions is one of the most critical competencies in STCW exams and real sea life.

The combination of fixed bearing + decreasing range indicates the risk of collision. Calculating the close passage point (CPA) and TCPA of the other ship with the relative vector on the ARPA is the most accurate way to determine the time required for the give-way maneuver. In practice, it is standard to take action when TCPA > 15 minutes; Leaving it later may force the stand-on ship to perform a Rule 17(b) manoeuvre. It is sometimes difficult to determine which ship is 'starboard' in the rule: if two ships are on almost the same course and intersect at a small angle difference, the head-on–crossing distinction can create a gray zone.

CSS Code, denizin asla durağan olmadığı: CSS Code arises from the fact that the sea is never static. The ship lurches, shakes fore and aft, and is thrown around; These movements impose an inertial force on the cargo that is multiples of the ship's own weight. An inadequately secured load will slip, tip over or fall overboard; this could be both fatal to the crew and devastating to the stability of the ship. The code establishes general principles and calculation methods for safe stowing and lashing of cargo. Each ship must carry and implement a Cargo Securing Manual (CSM) specific to its type and the types of cargo it carries.

CSS Code'un Ek 13 hesaplama yöntemi, gem: The Annex 13 calculation method of the CSS Code is based on numerically estimating the inertial force that ship motion exerts on the load. When the ship rolls and pitches at sea, every point on the deck is subjected to an angular acceleration and a corresponding linear acceleration; This acceleration is multiplied by the weight of the load at that point to obtain horizontal and vertical inertia forces, and the net force trying to shift or topple the load is calculated in this way. The most critical parameter of the calculation is the ship's metacentric height (GM): a ship with a high GM behaves 'stiff', that is, completes the roll quickly and with large angular acceleration, which magnifies the inertial forces on the deck load; A 'soft' (tender) ship with a low GM will make slower and larger rolls, the acceleration will be smaller, but an extremely low GM is dangerous in terms of stability. Therefore, lashing design must take into calculation the GM range of the ship in expected loading situations; The same load and the same lashing arrangement may have different safety margins at different GM values. Annex 13 formulates this relationship with standard motion coefficients and design wave conditions to produce the minimum cargo securing capacity required for each load position.

Cumulonimbus, tabanı deniz seviyesine ya: Cumulonimbus is a giant convective cloud whose base is close to sea level and whose top can reach the tropopause (12 km and above); Its top becomes flattened by icing and takes the characteristic anvil shape. It is the most dangerous cloud a sailor can encounter and can single-handedly produce the full range of severe weather events: thunder and lightning, sudden torrential downpours, hail, gusts that can exceed 50 knots, microbursts (downbursts) and tornadoes/waterspouts. The most critical danger is the gust front: cold downdraft within the Cb hits the surface and spreads, creating a sudden wind shift and intensification 10–15 miles ahead of the cloud, before precipitation begins. The wind direction may turn up to 180 degrees as Cb approaches. CBs come in single cells or organized as squall lines in front of the cold front.

Cumulus, düz tabanlı, karnabahar görünüm: Cumulus is a flat-bottomed, cauliflower-looking, white cluster cloud with sharp edges. It grows on thermals formed by daytime heating or by the passage of a cold air mass over a warm sea. Diffused cumulus (cumulus humilis) whose horizontal dimension is greater than its vertical dimension is a 'fair weather cumulus': it indicates that the atmosphere is slightly unstable but healthy, visibility is good and the weather will remain clear. However, what needs to be monitored is vertical growth: the rise of the cumulus tower beyond its height during the day (cumulus congestus / towering cumulus, TCu) indicates that the atmosphere is suitable for deep convection and that showers may develop within 30–60 minutes and Cb may develop within a few hours.

D-2 standardını karşılayan bir Balast Su: A Ballast Water Treatment System that meets the D-2 standard operates not as a single device, but as a production line consisting of complementary stages. The first stage is usually a mechanical filtration unit; While ballast is being removed, it separates large particles, sediment and macroscopic organisms from the water through a washable sieve, thus reducing the treatment load and increasing the efficiency of the next stage. The second stage is disinfection and is implemented through one of three main technologies: UV radiation disrupts cell DNA, preventing organisms from multiplying; Electrochlorination disinfects the salt in seawater by converting it to sodium hypochlorite by electrolysis and producing active chlorine; Ozonation breaks down the cell structure with ozone gas, which is a strong oxidant. Before discharge, usually a neutralization step (in chlorine-based systems) reduces the residual oxidant level below the discharge limit. To prove that the system actually delivers D-2 performance after installation, commissioning testing is carried out: an independent sampling team samples the intake and discharge waters during the actual ballast operation and validates the viable organism count (for size classes >50 μm and 10-50 μm) and bacterial indicators in the laboratory. Without passing this test, the certificate is not issued and the system is not considered D-2 compliant.
D-2 standardını sağlamak için balast suy: Ballast water treatment systems are used to meet the D-2 standard. Common technologies: filtration + killing/inactivating organisms with ultraviolet (UV); filtration + electrochlorination/chemical disinfection (active substance). The system is activated during ballast intake and/or discharge. Sediments (sludge containing organisms that accumulate at the bottom of the tank) are regularly managed and disposed of appropriately. Correct operation and calibration of the BWMS is critical to ensure that discharge remains within legal limits.

An error in measuring the volume or density of a bunker delivery, an incorrect reading of a tank sounder in rough seas, or a flowmeter drifting out of calibration over time (flowmeter drift) will result in a different amount of fuel being reported than actually consumed; This difference directly distorts the calculation of annual CO₂ emissions and therefore the CII rate (AER). Demirin tutması büyük ölçüde zincirin de: The holding of the anchor depends largely on the chain applying a HORIZONTAL pull along the seabed. The length of chain paid out (scope) must therefore be several times the depth of water. In good weather the usual rule is chain of about 5–6 times the depth; more (7+ times) is paid out in bad weather. The weight of the chain (catenary) keeps the pull horizontal and increases the holding power.
Demirin tutması, yeterli kaloma (salınan: The anchor holds when sufficient scope (paid-out chain length / water depth ratio) is given. A significant portion of the chain lying horizontally on the bottom increases holding by pulling the anchor flukes horizontally rather than upwards. The general rule of thumb is to pay out about 5–6 times the depth in normal conditions, and 8–10 times or more in heavy weather. Insufficient scope increases the risk of the anchor dragging. The type of bottom also matters: mud/clay holds well, rock and hard sand may hold poorly or foul the anchor.

Denetimde bulunan her eksiklik standart: Each deficiency found during the inspection is recorded with standard codes and an action is assigned: some are corrected on site, some are postponed to the next port or for a certain period of time. The most severe consequence is detention: the ship is detained from sailing until serious deficiencies are corrected and suffers commercial losses during this period. Repeated detentions may lead to a regional ban on the ship. The consequences are not limited to single ships: detentions affect the flag state's White/Grey/Black list ranking, which determines the inspection frequency of all ships of that flag. That's why ships carry out internal inspection (pre-PSC) before entering the port and close the deficiencies in advance.
Denetimde bulunan her eksiklik, standart: Each deficiency found in the audit is recorded with a standardized code and a corrective action is assigned to it. Some deficiencies are corrected on the spot (code 10), some are postponed to be corrected at the next port (code 15) or within a certain period of time (code 16, e.g. 14 days), some are notified to the flag state or classification society (code 17/45). The most severe action is detention (code 30): the ship cannot leave the port until serious deficiencies have been corrected and it is safe. Deficiencies are grouped into 17 main categories (certificates, structural safety, fire safety, lifesaving, navigational safety, MARPOL, ISM, ISPS, MLC, BWM, etc.) and contain hundreds of subcodes. This standardization ensures that auditors in every port of the world speak the same language and that results are shared consistently in regional databases (THETIS, APCIS).

Therefore, class management is a permanent and non-negligible part of ship management. Special survey regimes such as ESP and dry dock inspection are also part of this framework.

Designated Person Ashore (DPA), ISM Code: Designated Person Ashore (DPA) is the ISM Code's most unique corporate innovation: it aims to establish a direct, unfiltered line of communication between the ship and the company's top management. What the rule clearly requires is that the DPA has direct access to the highest level of management of the company; This means the DPA is not trapped within the hierarchy of operational or commercial departments, nor dependent on the approval of a supervisor with a commercial or operational conflict of interest when reporting a safety concern. The logic behind this access requirement is clear: when a Master reports a safety risk, this information should not be filtered internally and mitigated by commercial considerations such as 'not delaying the voyage' or 'not increasing cost'. The role of the DPA in daily practice is largely proactive rather than reactive: it monitors internal audit results, analyzes near-miss and non-conformity reports, conveys concerns from the ship to senior management and, when necessary, defends the company's resource allocation decisions (personnel, maintenance budget, equipment renewal) in line with safety requirements. When this independence of the DPA is weakened, ISM auditors often identify this as the system's most vulnerable point.
