Metasentrik yükseklik ise ağırlık merkez: Metacentric height refers to the vertical distance between the center of gravity and the metacentric point and is denoted by GM. This distance directly determines whether the ship will behave stable or unstable at a small angle of heel. When the metacentric height is positive, the metacentric point is located above the center of gravity and the ship is considered stable. When the metacentric height is zero, the center of gravity and the metacentric point coincide and the ship is in indifferent equilibrium. When the metacentric height is negative, the metacentric point remains below the center of gravity and the ship behaves unstable.

MLC 2006, beş Title etrafında örgütlenir: MLC 2006 is organized around five Titles, each securing a different dimension of the seafarer's life. Title 1 establishes the minimum conditions for work on board: minimum age (16, with stricter limits for night and hazardous work), valid health certificate, vocational training and regulated recruitment/placement services. Title 2 covers the conditions of employment: written Maritime Employment Agreement (SEA), regular wage payment, working/rest hours, leave entitlement and repatriation. Title 3 governs the fact that the ship is a living space: cabin, ventilation, lighting, dining and recreation standards. Title 4 covers health protection, medical care, occupational safety and social security. Title 5 regulates compliance and implementation (certification, audit, complaint mechanisms). Each Title consists of binding Standards (Part A) and guiding Guidelines (Part B).
MLC 2006, denizcilerin onurlu ve adil ko: MLC 2006 provides for seafarers to work in dignified and fair conditions. The D&A process must be conducted in accordance with the principles of confidentiality, registration and fair consideration, even while applying zero tolerance; Otherwise, it creates both legal and reputational risks.

MLC 2006, gıdanın yeterli miktar, besin: MLC 2006 requires food to be provided in sufficient quantity, nutritional value, quality and variety and free of charge. Budget discipline is no excuse for lowering this standard; the cook balances the two together.
MLC 2006, mürettebata yeterli ve güvenli: MLC 2006 requires crews to be provided with adequate and safe drinking water; Water quality should be monitored and hygiene records kept.
MLC 2006, SOLAS, MARPOL ve STCW'nin yanı: MLC 2006 sits alongside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW as the 'fourth pillar' of maritime law; because while the former regulate the ship and professional qualifications, the MLC directly protects the humane working and living conditions of the seafarer. It combines 68 separate conventions and recommendations within the ILO into a single consolidated text. Its structure is built around five Titles, and each Title consists of binding Standards (Part A) and guiding Guidelines (Part B). The strength of the convention comes from the principle of 'no more favorable treatment', which subjects a ship to both flag state inspection and port state control: even a ship of a flag that has not ratified the MLC is inspected in an MLC member port.

MLC 2006'nın tasarımında bilinçli bir es: There is deliberate flexibility in the design of the MLC 2006: rather than imposing the same rigid pattern on each country's legal system, administrative structure and existing legislation, the convention allows different means of implementation that achieve the same protective goal. This is called 'substantial equivalence' and is embodied in DMLC Part I. For example, a standard may stipulate a certain minimum square footage of seafarer accommodation; Instead of strictly applying this minimum square metre, a country may adopt an alternative regulation (e.g. a different space-to-person ratio, additional common space compensation) adapted to its ship types and climatic conditions, but which equally protects the seafarer's overall quality of life and privacy; This is conditioned on the ILO being informed of the justification for this difference and demonstrating that the alternative provides 'exactly equal' protection of the standard. This flexibility is an important reason why the MLC has been able to bring more than 100 flag states around the world with different legal and shipbuilding traditions into the same contract; A rigid, one-dimensional set of standards would not find such broad acceptance.
MLC Certificate (Maritime Labour Certifi: MLC Certificate (Maritime Labor Certificate) is a certificate that certifies that a ship meets the working and living conditions standards within the scope of MLC 2006. While SOLAS certificates document the ship and STCW document the competence of the crew, the MLC Certificate directly ensures the humane working conditions of the seafarer. Mandatory for international expedition ships of 500 GT and above; It is issued by the flag state or authorized classification society after compliance with the 14 MLC control areas is verified. It is valid for five years and is subject to an interim audit in the middle of the term.

MLC sertifikasyonunda en sık denetlenen: The most frequently inspected and most frequently deficient area in MLC certification is working/rest hours. The rule applies with a limit of either maximum work (maximum 14 hours in 24 hours, maximum 72 hours in 7 days) or minimum rest (minimum 10 hours in 24 hours, minimum 77 hours in 7 days); The rest can be divided into two parts at most and one part should be at least 6 hours. These hours are recorded daily for each sailor and a copy is given to the sailor. It is essential that the records reflect reality: records that appear compliant on paper but actually conceal overwork are violations of both MLC and STCW and have serious consequences in the PSC inspection. These rules closely match the fatigue provisions of the STCW; because fatigue is both a seafarer's right issue and a direct safety risk.

Crew satisfaction surveys and menu rotation system directly affect morale on the ship.
MLC, dört bölgeden oluşan bir yapı üzeri: MLC is built on a structure consisting of four regions: Articles, Regulations, Code Part A (mandatory Standards) and Code Part B (guideline Guidelines). The Master is the implementer of this structure on the ship.
MLC, gemide ayrımcılığı yasaklar, adil ç: MLC prohibits discrimination on board, ensures fair working conditions and an on-board complaints procedure. The Master is responsible for establishing a functioning mechanism through which each crew member can submit complaints without fear of retaliation.
MLC, liman devleti kontrolünde en sık ek: MLC is one of the areas where port state control is most frequently lacking; because problems such as unpaid wages, overwork, insufficient food or poor accommodation are concrete and easily identified. Serious MLC violations may lead to detention of the ship. Additionally, the MLC gives the seafarer direct power: through grievance mechanisms on board and ashore, a seafarer can mobilize the port state and this can trigger an inspection. That's why ships keep DMLC Part II up to date, keep working hour records regularly and are always prepared for PSC MLC inspections.
MLC, mürettebata temiz, hijyenik ve sağl: The MLC requires crew to be provided with clean, hygienic and healthy living conditions. Bathroom/toilet hygiene, ventilation and sanitation are supervised by the PSC.
MLC'nin denizciyi en somut biçimde koruy: One of the provisions of the MLC that most concretely protects seafarers is the right to repatriation and the mandatory financial security that supports it. A seafarer must be returned to his country free of charge when his contract ends, he becomes ill, or the ship/company cannot fulfill its obligations. The financial security added by the 2014 amendments (usually through P&I insurance) comes into play in the event of shipowner bankruptcy or seafarer abandonment: it covers outstanding wages, repatriation costs and basic needs. The ship is required to keep certificates showing this financial assurance (e.g. separate documents for abandonment and death/long-term disability) visible on board; Their absence will result in a deficiency record in the PSC inspection. This mechanism is a response to past cases where seafarers were left unpaid and helpless in foreign ports for months.
MLC'nin gücü, denetlenebilir olmasından: The power of MLC comes from its auditability. International expedition ships of 500 GT and above must carry a Maritime Labor Certificate issued by the flag state and a two-part DMLC (Part I indicates state requirements, Part II indicates company measures); These are valid for five years and are subject to interim audit. The principle that strengthens the scope of the agreement is 'no more favorable treatment': even a ship of a flag that has not ratified the MLC is inspected in an MLC member port, so that substandard operators cannot take advantage. Grievance mechanisms that give direct power to the seafarer operate both on board and ashore and are protected against retaliation; A seafarer can trigger an inspection by reporting unpaid wages or poor conditions to the port state. The MLC is one of the most frequent areas of deficiencies in port state control, with serious violations leading to ship detention; Mandatory financial security added by the 2014 amendments comes into play in the event of bankruptcy of the shipowner or abandonment of the seafarer.

Monitoring is the final phase of the passage planning process and continues throughout the journey. At this stage, the compliance of the passage plan with the actual application conditions is regularly checked; When deviations are detected, the reasons are investigated and necessary corrective measures are taken. Monitoring is not a reactive alarm management; It is a proactive compliance monitoring process.

Navlun iki temel biçimde belirlenir. Ton: Freight is determined in two basic ways. Total revenue in freight per ton is the quantity of freight transported multiplied by the unit freight rate: Freight = Freight (tons) × Rate ($/ton). In lump sum freight, a fixed amount is paid for the entire ship or a certain capacity, regardless of the quantity carried; This protects the shipowner in situations where the cargo quantity is uncertain or the ship cannot be used to full capacity. The contract specifies which quantity (loaded or unloaded) will be taken into account and the tolerances.
Navlun mukavelesi (Contract of Affreight: Freight contract (COA) is based on the commitment to transport a certain amount of cargo in a certain period, not on a specific ship. The shipowner/operator carries the contracted cargo parties with suitable vessels (own or rented). COA secures the logistics of parties with large and regular cargo flows (e.g. miners, energy companies) while giving the operator flexibility in ship selection. The price is usually determined as freight per ton.
Navlun oranları arz-talep dengesiyle bel: Freight rates are determined by the balance of supply and demand; In the short run, supply is inelastic and therefore volatile.

Navlun oranları, taşıma talebi (dünya ti: Freight rates are determined by the balance between transport demand (world trade, product flows, seasonality) and ship supply (existing fleet, newbuild deliveries, scrapping). Rates rise rapidly when demand exceeds supply; because ship supply is inelastic in the short run (new ship construction takes years). Nimbostratus, koyu gri, kalın ve şekilsi: Nimbostratus is a dark gray, thick and amorphous precipitation cloud; Its base decreases below 2 km with rainfall and completely blocks the sun. The root 'nimbus' in its name suggests that it brings precipitation: it produces moderate and continuous rain or snow that lasts for hours, sometimes up to a day. Its difference from Cb showers is the character of the precipitation: Ns precipitation is continuous and does not include sudden wind changes, while Cb precipitation is short, heavy and gusty. The main risk of Ns to the sailor is visibility: precipitation and lowering of cloud base can reduce visibility to 1–3 miles; Fragmented stratus fractus (scud) clouds formed under the cloud further restrict visibility. OPRC metninin kendisi 'Tier 1/2/3' terim: The OPRC text itself does not use the term 'Tier 1/2/3', but the structure that the convention imposes on national emergency plans is commonly applied in the industry with this tiered logic. At the lowest level are small-scale leaks that the ship can respond to with its own SOPEP equipment (limited amounts of sorbents, booms and dispersants); At this stage, intervention is initiated by the ship crew within minutes. When a spill exceeds the ship's own capacity, larger volume booms, recovery vessels and storage units in regional stockpile centers (held by port operators, national coastal protection agencies or industry consortiums) come into play; This level can reach the field within hours. In the largest-scale events (such as a major tanker accident), national capacity may also be insufficient and the international mutual aid mechanisms envisaged by the OPRC will be activated; This involves other states sending expert teams, specialized equipment, and even response ships to the scene. National emergency plans pre-define the transition thresholds and trigger decisions between these three levels.
OPRC-HNS Protokolü'nün pratikte petrol s: The point where the OPRC-HNS Protocol differs from oil spill response in practice is that the physical and toxicological behavior of hazardous and harmful substances (cargoes such as acids, solvents, liquefied gas carried by chemical tankers) is very different from oil. While oil can spread on the water surface and be surrounded by the boom, some HNS substances dissolve in water, sink, evaporate, or react with water to release toxic gas; This makes standard boom and sorbent equipment often useless. HNS response therefore requires different equipment and expertise: vapor suppression systems, chemical-specific personal protective equipment (at a much higher level of protection than the standard oil response suit), gas detectors and substance-specific neutralization agents. Due to the cost and infrequent use of this specialized capacity, a significant portion of the world's ports do not have HNS response capacity, although they are proficient in oil spill response; This gap requires shipowners operating chemical tankers to investigate in advance which ports can offer real HNS response support in route planning.
OPRC'nin gemi düzeyindeki somut çıktısı,: The tangible output of the OPRC at the ship level is the emergency response plan that every ship carries: SOPEP for oil and SMPEP, its integrated version combining oil and hazardous materials. These plans describe step-by-step who will do what, which valve to close, where the equipment is located, and who to call in the event of a leak. Notification is vital: a pollution incident must be reported immediately to the nearest coastal state, in a standard format (pollution type, estimated quantity, weather/sea conditions, actions taken); Early notification enables response resources to be mobilized in a timely manner.

Paralel indeks (Parallel Index), radar v:
Parallel Index is a navigation tracking technique that plots parallel to the planned course line on the radar or ECDIS and continuously shows the horizontal distance between the ship and a fixed reference point (usually a prominent shore point, cape, lighthouse or radar reflector). The technique is very simple in essence: the ship's distance to a certain point is kept under control at all times by drawing a line parallel to the course line according to the position of that point on the radar or ECDIS screen.

The parallel index is one of the most critical navigation tools of the bridge, especially in narrow straits, approach routes of ports, shallow waters and situations where visibility is limited. Thanks to this technique, the officer can instantly see how much he has deviated from the planned route; Small deviations can interfere before they become larger. The fact that it can be applied with radar, even without a visual cue or if the GPS is corrupted, increases the reliability of the technique.

Parallel index implementation is based on the principle that the only truly useful navigation control is instantaneous, continuous, and visual verification. Just knowing the ship's position is not enough; It is necessary to make sure that the ship is moving in the right direction and at the right distance. Therefore, IMO and STCW legislation define the parallel index technique as a mandatory component of bridge qualification programmes.

Paralel indeks uygulamasında şu adımlar: The following steps are followed in the parallel index application: (1) Before the journey, the most appropriate reference point for each critical section of the route is selected on the chart and the planned distances are measured. (2) These distances are recorded in the PI table or plan note and transferred at watch handover. (3) During navigation, the reflection of the reference point is detected on the screen and the PI line is adjusted to show that reflection. (4) If the reference point lags behind the line, the ship is moving away from the planned route; If it's in front of you, it means it's getting closer.

The planned horizontal distance between the ship and this reference point is then measured; This distance is calculated in advance from the chart.

Paris MoU, liman devleti kontrolünün böl: The Paris MoU is the memorandum of understanding that invented regional coordination of port state control and became a model for the world. A single state's controls cover only its own ports; but ships operate regionally. The basic idea of the Paris MoU is that member states share audit results in a common database (THETIS) and divide the audit burden among them. Thus, when a ship is inspected in a member port, the result is visible to all members and substandard ships can be tracked throughout the region while unnecessary re-inspections are prevented. It covers one of the busiest maritime traffic regions in the world, with 27 member states.
Paris MoU'nun 2011'de uygulamaya koyduğu: The New Inspection Regime (NIR), introduced by the Paris MoU in 2011, forms the backbone of the modern PSC. To every ship; A risk profile is assigned based on type, age, flag performance, class (RO) performance, past inspection results and ISM/ISPS history. The ship is considered High (HRS), Standard (SRS) or Low (LRS) risk and inspection frequency is determined accordingly: high-risk ships are targeted every few months, low-risk ones every two to three years. In addition, Concentrated Inspection Campaigns (CIC) are conducted once or twice a year, focusing on a specific issue (e.g. BWM, STCW, fire safety).
Paris MoU'nun operasyonel beyni THETIS a: The operational brain of the Paris MoU is the information system called THETIS: the results of inspections at all member ports, ship risk profiles, detected deficiencies and detention records are collected in this central database and shared in real time. The system calculates which ship should be inspected based on its risk profile and provides target lists to inspectors; thus, audit effort is directed at the risk most. Each detected deficiency is recorded with standardized codes (17 main categories and hundreds of sub-codes) and an action is assigned to it. Thanks to this coding, a finding in one port becomes visible in another member port; A deficiency that needs to be corrected at the next port can be tracked and recurring findings can be revealed. THETIS is also integrated with the EU PSC Directive as THETIS-EU for EU member ports.
Paris MOU'nun risk endeksi; bayrak, sını: Risk index of Paris MOU; It is calculated based on flag, classification society, number of previous detentions and age.
Paris MoU'nun risk hedeflemesi yalnızca: The Paris MoU's risk targeting evaluates not only the ship but also the actors behind it. Flag state performance (White/Grey/Black list) as well as past performance of the ship operating company and the recognized organization (RO) that classifies the ship also enter into the risk profile: an operator or classification society that has caused a large number of detentions or deficiencies will have its ships inspected more frequently. This creates deterrence that spreads liability from a single ship across the entire fleet and service chain; Substandard management also becomes commercially expensive. Good performance is rewarded: ships reaching the low-risk profile (LRS) are inspected less frequently and the priority window is widened. Thus, the Paris MoU establishes a continuous quality pressure throughout the sector, beyond individual inspections.
The enforcement power of the Paris MoU is gradual. Serious deficiencies lead to detention of the ship; Repeated detentions lead to a ban—three detentions for three months, a fourth for twelve months, a fifth for twenty-four months, and then a permanent ban. Inspection performance also affects flag states: flags are divided into White, Gray and Black lists based on their three-year detention rates, and this ranking determines the likelihood of that flag's ships being inspected. Ships therefore monitor their risk profiles via THETIS, prepare for CIC themes and close deficiencies in advance.

The Master must collect all the evidence (photographs, records, survey reports) that will be the basis for the objection from the first moment.

Passage planning (route / voyage planning) is the comprehensive preparation process carried out before the navigation to ensure that the ship reaches the destination from the departure point safely, efficiently and in accordance with the legislation. IMO Resolution A.893(21) divides this process into four mandatory stages: Appraisal, Planning, Execution and Monitoring. This framework is also supported by SOLAS Chapter V; It creates a legal liability on the Master and navigation officers of all ships operating internationally.

The importance of route planning stems from the fact that it enables the bridge to operate 'proactively' rather than 'reactively' by identifying hazards and constraints in advance. When navigating without a plan, dangers are noticed as they approach; In these moments, both time and space for movement are limited. If there is a plan, the dangers are known well in advance, alternative decisions are made in advance, and the bridge can act decisively in times of crisis.

PDOP (Position Dilution of Precision) refers to the total geometric precision dilution in both horizontal and vertical position components of the GNSS receiver. PDOP is equal to the square root of the sum of the squares of HDOP and VDOP:

PDOP = √(HDOP² + VDOP²)

This relationship clearly shows that PDOP is always greater than or equal to HDOP; because when vertical uncertainty is added, the total position uncertainty increases. In marine navigation, PDOP provides an overview of 3D position accuracy; however, HDOP is usually the primary monitoring parameter.

Polar Code, buzlu sularda seyrin sıradan: The Polar Code arises from the fact that navigation in icy waters is radically different from ordinary sailing. In polar regions, ships face ice burdens, extremely low temperatures, long dark periods, limited mapping, poor communications and isolation where the nearest help can be days away. While an accident might be manageable in temperate waters, it could be fatal in the arctic. The Code therefore combines both safety (SOLAS Chapter
Polar Code, gemileri buzla başa çıkma ka: The Polar Code rates ships into seven Polar Classes (PC1-PC7) based on their ability to deal with ice; this is based on the IACS Unified Requirements. PC1 can operate year-round in the thickest perennial ice in all polar waters, while PC7 can only operate in thin first-year ice in summer. Higher classes require thicker hull sheet metal, reinforced frame structure, ice-reinforced propeller and rudder, and low-temperature steel. This classification combines ship categories: Category A operates in the harshest conditions (PC1-5), Category B operates in thinner ice (PC6-7), and Category C operates in open waters that do not require ice reinforcement. A ship may only sail in the ice and temperature conditions specified in its Polar Ship Certificate; This concretely limits which area the Master can enter and under what circumstances.
Polar Code, kutup sularında işletilen ge: The Polar Code imposes additional structural, equipment and operational requirements on ships operating in polar waters. The ship must carry a Polar Ship Certificate and maintain a Polar Water Operational Manual (PWOM) containing the ship's capacity/limits, risk assessment and operational procedures.

Pratikte head-on ile crossing arasındaki: In practice, the boundary between head-on and crossing is not always clear. Rule 14(c)'s 'in case of doubt assume head-on' principle is to manage this gray area. In ARPA, if two ships are seen approaching each other at more than 170–180°, head-on; If approaching above 90–135°, crossing; requires careful analysis. Pratikte tahıl yükleme kararı tek kişini: In practice, the decision to load grain is not the product of a single person, but of a pre-established approval chain. The ship's classification society or flag state approves a grain loading booklet containing stability calculations specific to the ship's geometry (hatch shape, longitudinal bulkheads, tank layout) and issues a Document of Authorization based on this; This document predefines under what occupancy conditions (full laden, partially laden, feeding applied) the ship can safely carry grain. Before loading, the chief officer calculates the overturning moment and residual stability by comparing the planned loading case with the reference cases in the booklet; This calculation is usually independently verified before the payload layout is agreed with the terminal, as even a small deviation from a reference case in the booklet can exceed the criteria. Loading grain without a valid Document of Authorization or booklet calculation specific to that voyage is unacceptable both commercially and legally: the port authority and P&I insurers may reject such loading, the flag state may initiate an investigation, and the ship may be detained under PSC inspection. Undocumented or unaccounted loading means taking grain to sea without knowing its true behavior, which directly defeats the Grain Code's raison d'être.

PSC denetçisinin gözünde DMLC Part I ile: DMLC Part I and Part II have very different weight in the eyes of the PSC auditor. Part I is essentially a summary of the national legislation of the flag state; It does not carry any new information for the auditor, because that legislation is already public and the auditor relies on the flag state to verify it. Part II has a completely different nature: it is a commitment in which the company writes in its own voice, 'we meet these requirements concretely with these procedures, this recording system, these responsible persons'. This commitment translates directly into a testable checklist in the auditor's hands: if Part II says 'working hours are logged with the following software', the auditor requests records of that software; If it says 'complaints are submitted in writing to this box', it asks whether that box exists and whether the crew is aware of it. That is, while Part I is accepted background information, not a fact that needs to be verified, Part II is a directly falsifiable claim — either it is confirmed or it collapses. This asymmetry is why PSC inspectors spend almost all MLC inspection energy looking for the actual onboard equivalent of Part II.

PSC denetimi tek tip değildir; bir piram: PSC supervision is not uniform; it deepens like a pyramid. Initial inspection checks the validity of certificates, the general condition of the ship and the basic compliance of the crew; most inspections start and end here. Radar (Radio Detection and Ranging), ele: Radar (Radio Detection and Ranging) is the primary collision avoidance and navigation device that determines the distance and bearing of surrounding ships, land and buoys by emitting electromagnetic pulses and measuring the reflections from targets. Target tracking, CPA/TCPA calculation and maneuver evaluation are performed with ARPA (Automatic Radar Plotting Aid). This section; It covers radar physics (pulse, frequency band, antenna), X-band and S-band difference, ARPA tracking and collision avoidance use, sea/rain clutter and interpretation errors, SOLAS equipment requirements and maintenance/malfunction in engineering depth.
Radar (Radio Detection And Ranging), mik:
Radar (Radio Detection And Ranging) is an active detection system that emits electromagnetic energy pulses in the microwave band (typically 3 GHz / S-band or 9 GHz / X-band) in the direction of the target and extracts the distance, bearing and movement information of the target by analyzing the reflected signal. Marine radar operates regardless of visibility; It can detect targets even in fog, rain, darkness or heavy sea spray conditions.

Maritime radar is the most critical electronic tool of the bridge. Under COLREG Rules 5 and 7, the use of radar is required for proper lookout and collision risk assessment. SOLAS Chapter V requires ships of 500 GT and above to have at least two independent radars. Modern ARPA (Automatic Radar Plotting Aid) systems automatically track targets, calculate CPA and TCPA and generate alarms on the risk of collision.

Radar mevki tayini (Radar Fixing), kıyı:
Radar fixing is the process of determining the exact position of the ship on the chart using radar distances and bearings taken from the coastline or significant objects. In situations where GPS access is not available or is questioned, radar fix provides an independent and reliable position source. Radar locator is also used to verify GPS position.

The main advantage of fixing with radar is that it is based on real-world reference: radar detects physical objects in real time and is not dependent on GPS or chart databases. Therefore, electronic chart errors or GPS distortions do not negatively affect the radar fix. However, radar measurements also have their own systematic and random errors; It is the navigator's responsibility to understand and minimize these errors.

Radar ölçümlerini etkileyen sistematik h: Systematic errors affecting radar measurements should be known and corrected if possible. Index error: the radar sets the distance zero incorrectly; It is determined by test procedures and a correction value is applied. Beam width error: the radar beam is a certain angular width; The reflection of large targets on the radar screen appears larger than the actual size, and an error occurs if the bearing measurement is made from the edge instead of the center. Reflection point selection: the point used in the distance fix must coincide with its location on the chart – if one end of the same object does not match the marked point on the chart, a systematic error occurs.

Radar paralel indeksi, köprüüstü seyir t:
Radar parallel index is one of the most practical and important applications of bridge navigation techniques. The basic idea is simple: a line is drawn on the radar screen representing the horizontal distance of a fixed reference point to the ship, and the ship tracks its position relative to this line throughout its course. As long as the reflection of the reference point on the radar screen remains above this line, the ship is on the correct course at the correct distance; Any deviation is immediately noticed visually.

Radar PI is the routine navigational monitoring tool of the bridge during coastal navigation, narrow strait crossings, port approaches and in limited visibility conditions. STCW qualification standards expect officers to have the ability to establish and interpret radar PI; MCA and IMO guidelines define this technique as an integral part of passage plan preparation.

Record of Equipment (Form E), sertifikan: Record of Equipment (Form E) is not a frozen list at the time the certificate is issued, but a living document that must be updated simultaneously with the ship's equipment. Whenever a liferaft is replaced, a fire extinguishing system is replaced or a navigational device is replaced by a different model, this change must be recorded on Form E and, if necessary, undergo class/flag approval. The consequence of this omission is not a mere bureaucratic deficiency: when the auditor cannot find equipment on Form E that is actually on board the ship, or fails to see an item listed on Form E on the ship, this discrepancy is recorded as a PSC finding in itself, because the accuracy of this list is precisely what the certificate assures. In practice, this means that equipment procurement and maintenance processes require close coordination between the technical department and the documentation process; If a spare part or equipment replacement is recorded in the purchase record but not reflected in Form E, a silently widening gap arises between the certificate and the actual situation, which often emerges at the most crucial moment, during an inspection or accident.

Housekeeping; It is not just a matter of aesthetic cleaning, but also a matter of direct life safety, inspection preparation and operational efficiency. A messy deck; It is the leading cause of slip-trip-fall accidents, blocked escape routes, inaccessible fire/lifesaving equipment, and PSC arrests. This section; It covers hatch cover operations, lashing/securing practice, hold preparation and cleaning, sounding and bilge support, on-deck cargo securing and operational safety in detail.

Rhumb line veya loxodrom, tüm meridyenle:
Rhumb line or loxodrome is the surface curve that intersects all meridians at a constant angle. In other words, if the ship always sails at the same angle (true course) to the north-south meridians, the line it follows is loxodrome. The practical consequence of this technical definition is extremely powerful: there is no need to change the route throughout the journey; The rudder is held steady.

In the Mercator projection, a loxodrome appears as a straight line connecting the start and end point. This feature is one of the main reasons that makes the Mercator chart the standard for sea navigation: it is possible to draw and read the route directly on the chart using a ruler and protractor. This practicality makes the loxodrome the preferred line format for short and medium distance cruising.

However, due to spherical geometry, loxodrome does not show the shortest path between two points. The shortest path is located on the great circle (orthodrome). The difference in distance between two lines can reach significant levels depending on the latitude and distance sailed; Especially in high latitudes and long transatlantic routes, this difference can reach hundreds of nautical miles.
Rhumb line, Mercator’da düz çizgi görünü: Rhumb line appears as a straight line in Mercator; This makes navigating a fixed course practical on the chart.
Rhumb line, özellikle yüksek enlemlerde: The rhumb line is longer than the great circle, especially at higher latitudes.

RightShip iki ana metrik üretir. Safety: RightShip produces two main metrics. Safety Score (Qi) is a safety risk score between 0.5 and 5.0; It is calculated by weighting factors such as the ship's accident/incident history, age, flag and class performance, PSC results and operator performance. A high score means low risk, and most charterers set a lower threshold (e.g. 2.5). The second metric is the GHG Rating: it gives an emissions efficiency rating from A to G based on the EVDI derived from the ship's design parameters. Thus, RightShip combines both safety and environmental aspects in a single business decision interface; The GHG Rating creates commercial pressure in line with the IMO's CII regime.
RightShip kuruldu (BHP Billiton, Rio Tin: RightShip established (BHP Billiton, Rio Tinto, Cargill)
RightShip'i SIRE veya PSC ile aynı kateg: A common misconception is to put RightShip in the same category as SIRE or PSC. PSC is a statistical system run by states that monitors minimum compliance with international conventions (SOLAS, MARPOL, MLC); SIRE, on the other hand, is a very in-depth and physical inspection specific to the oil majors' own tanker fleet. RightShip, on the other hand, neither exercises government authority nor conducts physical inspections as standard (physical Dry Bulk Inspection is exceptional and targeted); Its main function is to combine existing data (PSC history, classification records, accident reports) and produce a constantly updated commercial risk score. This difference has tangible consequences: a ship may have a clean record at PSC and valid SIRE approval, but due to a past accident record or poor class performance rating, may have a low RightShip Safety Score and be rejected by bulk charterers. The opposite is also possible: a ship that scores well on RightShip may receive serious operational observations in a current SIRE audit. These three systems are not interchangeable, they are overlapping but independent layers that reflect different time periods (RightShip historical data, SIRE current statutory, PSC current minimum compliance) and different usage purposes.
RightShip'in gerçek gücü, puanın kendisi: The real power of RightShip is not in the score itself, but in how that score is embedded into the chartering processes of large freight owners. Large grain and mineral traders, mining companies and oil companies set a minimum Qi threshold (often 4 and above, higher for some sensitive cargoes) in their corporate policies and build this threshold into their rental systems as a hard filter. The consequence of this is mechanical: a ship below the threshold cannot even be submitted as an offer to that company's broker, because it is automatically eliminated by the system. This is a different form of exclusion than PSC detention; The ship may not have violated any rules, but its commercial access was blocked by a software threshold. This structure makes RightShip an invisible front door to the charter pool rather than a regulatory agency, forcing shipowners to manage risk knowing that a PSC hold or accident record will leave a mark on the score for a long time.

Riyadh MoU bölgesi, dünya petrol ve gaz: The Riyadh MoU area is the heart of world oil and gas exports; therefore the inspection focus is mainly on tankers (crude oil, product, chemical, LNG/LPG). The region's semi-enclosed and shallow waters (Persian Gulf, Red Sea) are particularly sensitive to pollution and invasive species; This leads to MARPOL Special Area rules and ballast water management coming to the fore in the audit. High temperature and salinity can affect equipment performance and the effectiveness of ballast water treatment systems, so these conditions are also taken into account. Tankers entering the region must ensure that, in addition to standard PSC preparation, the inert gas system, cargo security and environmental equipment are working perfectly; because both PSC and commercial vetting focus on these elements.
Riyadh MoU bölgesinin denetim öncelikler: The most concrete geographical fact that determines the control priorities of the Riyadh MoU region is that almost all maritime traffic leaving the Persian Gulf has to pass through the narrow and shallow waters of the Strait of Hormuz. Considering that world crude oil trade and a significant volume of LNG pass through this corridor, both the environmental and geopolitical consequences of a single accident or pollution event would be large-scale. The audit focus of the Riyadh MoU therefore gives disproportionate weight to tanker safety and pollution prevention beyond the scope of the general PSC: inert gas systems, cargo tank safety equipment, oil-water separators and ballast water management are items specifically questioned in routine inspections. The narrow passage corridor of the Bosphorus and heavy tanker traffic also require strict supervision of navigational safety and bridge procedures; Any deficiency affecting a tanker's maneuverability or navigational equipment carries a disproportionate risk in these narrow waterways. As a result, PSC preparation for tankers and LNG ships entering the region should be more comprehensive and cargo/environment-oriented than for other ship types.

Riyadh MoU, Basra Körfezi, Arap Denizi v: The Riyadh MoU coordinates port state control of six Gulf countries (Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE) in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea and Red Sea region. The region is a strategic corridor through which a significant part of the world's oil traffic passes; therefore the MoU focuses specifically on oil and chemical tankers. Although it is a relatively new and smaller organization compared to other major MoUs, it enforces auditing standards in line with the IMO PSC Guidelines (Res. A.1138(31)) and provides regional data sharing.
Riyadh MoU, Paris veya Tokyo MoU'ya kıya: The Riyadh MoU is a regional regime with both fewer members and younger institutional maturity compared to the Paris or Tokyo MoU; This means that the audit capacity and data infrastructure have not yet reached the same level of maturity. To close this gap, the MoU makes extensive use of IMO's technical cooperation programmes: auditor training, adoption of common audit guidelines and full compliance with the IMO PSC Guidelines (Res. A.1138(31)) are central to this effort. At the same time, the Riyadh MoU seeks to gradually harmonize its regional information system and deficiency/withholding criteria with the more established practices of the Paris and Tokyo MoU; This ensures that inspection results are internationally comparable and makes it easier for ships calling in the region to be prepared to a single consistent standard. The relatively small number of members can actually turn out to be an advantage: the adoption of new practices and common guidelines can be relatively rapid compared to larger and dispersed MoUs. Over time, this harmonization aims to achieve a control capacity appropriate to the strategic importance of the region.

RO'ya devredilen sörvey ve sertifikasyon: The survey and certification authority delegated to the RO does not relieve the flag state of its responsibility; It is only the actual performance of the work that is delegated, with ultimate accountability always remaining with the flag state. When an RO issues a certificate on behalf of a flag state, this certificate legally has the signature of the flag state on the back; When faulty or lax surveying by the RO leads to PSC detention or an accident, the problem does not remain a single RO incident, but is reflected in the IMSAS audit and overall performance report of the flag state authorizing that RO. Flag states must therefore manage their relationship with their ROs not as a one-way delegation of authority but as an agency relationship that must be constantly monitored: this includes regularly reviewing RO performance data (detection rates, delays, recurring deficiencies), conducting annual evaluations, and, where necessary, limiting or completely withdrawing an RO's authority for certain types of certificates or geographical areas. RO Code establishes this control relationship as bilateral accountability: RO is accountable to the flag state, and the flag state is accountable to IMO. In practice, this means that a well-managed flag actually audits its ROs, while a poorly managed flag leaves certification entirely to the RO and does no verification itself; the latter case sooner or later becomes visible in IMSAS and therefore in PSC statistics.

Rota ölçümü ile birlikte sıkça kullanıla: One of the concepts frequently used with course measurement is counter course. Countercourse of a route means following the same line in the opposite direction and is found by adding or subtracting 180° to the actual course value.
Rota ölçümü, deniz haritası üzerinde bel: Course measurement is the process of finding the angular value of the direction between two points determined on the sea chart, relative to true north. This process is the concrete equivalent of the concept of direction in navigation on the chart and is mandatory for all speed-time-distance calculations to be applied in a correct direction. Route measurement is not just reading an angle; The projection of the chart, the meridian structure and the correct reference of the measurement tool used are integral parts of this process.
Rota ölçümü, denizcilikte en temel işlem: Although route measurement seems to be one of the most basic operations in maritime, it is one of the most error-prone issues. Incorrect reference line, angle reading in the wrong direction, or using the wrong scale chart can invalidate the entire passage plan. Therefore, route measurement is not a mechanical ruler movement; It should be considered as a conscious process in which the concept of direction, chart structure and mathematical discipline are applied together.
Rota ölçümü, mesafe ölçümü, ölü hesap me: Route measurement, distance measurement, dead reckoning position advancement, bearing intersection and all classical navigation calculations made on the chart work with the Mercator projection assumption. Without this projection, no direct relationship could be established between the straight line on the chart and the course taken at sea.
Rota ölçümünde harita projeksiyonunun et: The effect of chart projection should also be taken into account in route measurement. In the Mercator projection, directions appear as straight lines; This is a huge advantage for fixed route navigation. However, as the distance between meridians increases at high latitudes, measurement accuracy may decrease. In these regions, route measurement should be done more carefully and, if possible, larger scale charts should be preferred.
Rota ölçümünün her zaman uygun ölçekli h: Route measurement should always be done on a chart of appropriate scale. The route measured on a small-scale chart may be sufficient for general navigation; However, this route should not be used in narrow waters and port approaches without using large-scale charts. The same route line may overlap shoals or obstacles on the large-scale chart.
Rota ölçümünün temel mantığı, ölçülecek: The basic logic of route measurement is based on finding the clockwise angle between the route line to be measured and a meridian direction. This angle is expressed between 0° and 360°. The reference line used during measurement must be a meridian; Parallel lines or the chart edge can be used as a reference only as long as they are parallel to the meridian direction.
Rota planlama kalitesi, köprüüstü yöneti: The quality of route planning is one of the true tests of bridge management. When the first bearing is taken, the ship's position is on this line, but its exact position is uncertain. The intersection of this advanced LOP and the second LOP is the running fix.
Running Fix, aynı sabit objeden farklı z: Running Fix is the assignment of position by transferring two or more bearings taken from the same fixed object at different times, taking into account the progress of the ship. It is a practical solution when the number of celestial objects is limited or simultaneous observation is not possible due to weather conditions.
Running Fix, tek bir sabit objeden farkl: Running Fix is a method of determining the position by moving two (or more) LOPs taken at different times from a single fixed object as far as the ship's course and the distance traveled. Wind creates two basic hydrodynamic effects on the ship: drag force and lift force. The combination of these two forces affects the course, speed and maneuverability of the ship at sea. Wind effect should be considered as a critical variable both in offshore navigation planning and during maneuvers in ports.

The effect of wind on the ship depends on the ship's freeboard height (side surface area above the water), superstructure shape and loading condition. In the empty ship (ballast) condition, the wind effect is much more pronounced since the freeboard is high; Since the waterline is high and the freeboard is low on a loaded ship, the wind effect is relatively reduced.

Safety Construction Certificate (SCC): c: Safety Construction Certificate (SCC): certifies under SOLAS that the ship's structure complies with the standards.
Safety Construction Certificate, bir gem: The Safety Construction Certificate certifies that a ship's structural and mechanical foundation complies with SOLAS Chapter II-1 (structure, compartmentation, stability, machinery, electrical) and II-2 (fire integrity) requirements. While other SOLAS certifications address equipment and operation, this certification ensures the 'skeleton' of the ship: covering the strength of the hull, watertight compartmentation, damage stability and structural bulkheads that limit the spread of fire. It is usually issued by the classification society on behalf of the flag state (as RO) because the issues evaluated directly overlap with the structural expertise of the classification.
Safety Construction Certificate, geminin: The Safety Construction Certificate reflects the approved structural condition of the ship at the time of construction or the last major renovation; Any significant intervention that changes this situation undermines the foundation on which the certificate is based. Structural changes, such as adding a new cabin block to the ship's upper deck, converting an existing open space into a closed volume, or relocating a watertight partition, directly affect the ship's subdivision scheme, damage stability calculations, fire partition plan or total weight distribution. Prior approval of the class and flag state must be obtained before such an intervention is carried out; After approval, a survey is conducted to verify that the change actually meets the requirements of SOLAS Chapter II-1/II-2, and the certificate is reconfirmed or updated according to the results of this survey. A 'silent' modification before this process is completed effectively invalidates the certificate; because the document no longer accurately reflects the actual structural condition of the ship. PSC inspectors look for signs of unauthorized modification, especially on older ships, by comparing the plan information in the certificate with the physical arrangement they observe on the ship; Such non-compliance is recorded as a serious deficiency.
Safety Construction Certificate'ın kapsa: The most critical issue covered by the Safety Construction Certificate is the ship's ability to survive damage. Watertight bulkheads divide the ship into compartments and ensure that the ship remains buoyant and stable when one or more compartments take on water; Damage stability calculations must prove that the ship will remain without sinking or overturning in certain damage scenarios. Watertight doors, bulkhead penetrations and bilge wells maintain this integrity; The approved stability information booklet shows in which loading situations the ship will remain safely balanced and is kept on board. The double bottom and reinforced structural members prevent a single damage from sinking the entire ship in a domino effect. Since these requirements directly coincide with the structural expertise of the classification society, the certificate is usually issued by the classification society on behalf of the flag.

The line between the scope of the Safety Construction Certificate and the scope of the Safety Equipment Certificate and SMC reflects the basic logic of maritime certification architecture: the ship's fixed, permanent 'hardware' and its mobile/replaceable equipment and management systems are secured by separate documents. The Safety Construction Certificate covers the physical framework and permanently installed systems of the ship, such as the hull, bulkheads, main machinery, electrical distribution and fire compartments; These are elements that are difficult to change, expensive and require structural approval. The Safety Equipment Certificate covers portable or replaceable equipment such as liferafts, fire extinguishers and navigational devices; these have more frequent service, replacement and renewal cycles. SMC, on the other hand, secures not any physical equipment, but how this equipment is managed, with what procedures it is operated, and how the crew implements these procedures. This tripartite division is not arbitrary: each requires different inspection expertise (structural engineering, equipment standards, management system inspection) and a different renewal/service rhythm; Combining them into a single certificate would not only complicate the audit process, but also cause a change in one area (e.g. a refit) to unnecessarily reopen other areas (structural approval).

Safety Radio Certificate, bir geminin te: The Safety Radio Certificate certifies that a ship's radio equipment complies with the requirements of SOLAS Chapter IV and GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System). The basic idea of GMDSS is to guarantee that a ship's distress call reaches the relevant rescue centers automatically and under all circumstances. Equipment requirements are determined by the sea area in which the ship sails: in A1 near the coast, VHF DSC is sufficient, while A3/A4 ships sailing in the open ocean must also carry HF or satellite (Inmarsat) systems. Thus, each ship has the minimum equipment to call for help from its location.
Safety Radio Certificate'ın temel mantığ: The basic logic of the Safety Radio Certificate is to determine the ship's radio equipment according to the sea area in which it sails; Because the system through which the distress call can be transmitted depends on its location. A1 is coastal waters within range of a VHF DSC coast station and VHF DSC is sufficient. A2 adds the range of an MF DSC station. A3 covers the high seas under satellite (Inmarsat) or HF coverage, A4 covers polar regions outside satellite coverage and requires HF DSC. Each area creates a layered structure by adding new equipment to the previous one. Mandatory GMDSS equipment; Includes VHF/MF/HF DSC, Inmarsat-C, EPIRB, SART/AIS-SART, NAVTEX and security message receivers. SAR sisteminin operasyonel kalbi, bir du: The operational heart of the SAR system is that it classifies the severity of a situation into three progressively increasing stages. INCERFA (uncertainty phase) comes into play in cases of doubt that are not yet alarming, such as failure to receive the expected report or news from a ship within a reasonable period of time; At this stage, MRCC collects information by contacting the responsible agencies and the ship. If the situation remains unclear or worsens, ALERFA (alert phase) is declared; This is the stage when serious concern arises about the safety of the ship or person and search and rescue resources are prepared. When it is understood that a serious and imminent danger is certain or that immediate help is required, DETRESFA (danger stage) is declared and a full-scale search and rescue operation is initiated. Coordination throughout these three phases operates in a hierarchical manner: the MRCC responsible for the SRR undertakes overall coordination, a SAR Mission Coordinator (SMC) carries out the day-to-day management of the operation depending on the size of the incident, and an On-Scene Coordinator (OSC) is appointed among the units actually present at the scene, managing the search order, sector sharing and communications traffic in the field. This three-tiered structure (MRCC-SMC-OSC) safely manages the distance between decision-making and actual execution in large-scale or long-term operations.
SAR Sözleşmesi devlet yükümlülüklerini d: Although the SAR Convention regulates state obligations, in practice the first responder is often the commercial ship closest to the scene. Therefore, the Master's obligation to assist persons in danger is reinforced by SOLAS V/33. For ships, this means keeping the MRCC contact information of passed SRRs ready, testing the alarm functions of GMDSS devices, verifying the operability of EPIRB and SART, and practicing man overboard (MOB) manoeuvres. Operational details are defined in the IAMSAR Manual, which combines maritime and aviation rescue; The SAR Convention provides the framework and IAMSAR provides the implementation manual.
SAR Sözleşmesi, bir durumun ne zaman ve: The SAR Convention defines three distress stages when and how a situation requires intervention. The uncertainty phase (INCERFA) is a state of doubt such as not receiving the expected news from a ship or person. The alarm phase (alert/ALERFA) is when uncertainty persists and anxiety increases; At this stage, search preparations are started. Distress phase (DETRESFA) is a situation in which a ship or person is in serious and imminent danger and requires immediate assistance. The MRCC takes action with increasing intensity at each stage: gathering information, alerting vehicles in the area and, when necessary, launching a full search-and-rescue operation. The search is systematically planned using standard search methods (expanding square, sector, parallel scan) based on the current possible location (datum) where the victim is carried by the current and wind.
SAR Sözleşmesinin devlet düzeyinde kurdu: The organized structure established by the SAR Convention at the state level works hand in hand with a much older principle of maritime law, the Master's obligation to assist persons in danger. This obligation is reinforced by SOLAS Chapter V, Regulation 33: the master of every ship who receives a distress signal or sees a person/ship in distress at sea must seek assistance as quickly as possible, unless doing so would put his ship, crew or passengers at serious risk; This obligation is independent of the ship's flag or the nationality of the parties involved. The same principle is also included in UNCLOS Article 98 and customary law. In practice, this means that in most distress situations the first response comes from the commercial ship closest to the scene and not from state SAR assets; Therefore, the SAR Convention regularizes this assistance by including commercial ships within the MRCC coordination. A Master immediately notifies MRCC of the situation while en route to assistance, MRCC may place him under the direction of the OSC as an official SAR asset, and he will be obligated to remain on scene until the ship completes its mission or another unit takes over. Thus, individual moral/legal obligation and the state's organized SAR system combine in a single operational chain.

One aspect of the Convention that has strengthened over time is the obligation to deliver persons rescued at sea (especially in cases of mass migration and refugee rescue) to a safe place; The coordination between the Master's obligation to assist and the coastal states' responsibility to accept the rescued persons is regulated in this context. Sayısal örnek: 100 mm çaplı çelik boruda: Numerical example: Water flows at 3 m/s in a 100 mm diameter steel pipe (ε = 0.045 mm), Re = 300000. ε/D = 0.045/100 = 0.00045. f ≈ 0.018 is read from the Moody diagram. For 50 m pipe with Darcy–Weisbach hf = 0.018 × (50/0.1) × (9/19.62) = 0.018 × 500 × 0.459 = 4.13 m.
Sayısal örnek: 100 mm iç çaplı boruda la: Numerical example: If water passes in laminar flow in a pipe with an inner diameter of 100 mm and the average speed is 0.5 m/s, Vmax = 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 m/s at the center. The flow rate is calculated as Q = A·Vort = π/4 × 0.1² × 0.5 = 3.93 × 10⁻³ m³/s = 3.93 L/s.
Sayısal örnek: 200 m uzunluğunda, 150 mm: Numerical example: In a 200 m long, 150 mm diameter steel pipeline, if the flow speed is 2 m/s and the friction factor f = 0.02, the continuous loss is hf = f·(L/D)·(V²/2g) = 0.02 × (200/0.15) × (4/19.62) = 0.02 × 1333.3 × 0.204 = 5.44 m.
Sayısal örnek: 4000 DWT bir gemide balas: Numerical example: On a 4000 DWT ship, if the ballast pump capacity is 300 m³/h and the total ballast capacity is 1200 m³, the full loading time is calculated as = 1200/300 = 4 hours.
Sayısal örnek: 50 mm çaplı bir boruda 20: Numerical example: Water at 20°C (ν = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s) flows at a speed of 0.03 m/s in a 50 mm diameter pipe. Re = V·D/ν = 0.03 × 0.05 / (1.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 1500. Since Re < 2300, the flow is laminar.
Sayısal örnek: Ana makine 8000 kW gücünd: Numerical example: If the main engine has a power of 8000 kW and 15% of the waste heat is transferred to the HT cooling water, Q = 0.15 × 8000 = 1200 kW. If the cooling water is ΔT = 10°C, the required flow rate is ṁ = Q/(cp·ΔT) = 1200/(4.18 × 10) = 28.7 kg/h = 103 m³/h.
Sayısal örnek: Bir boru hattında 4 adet: Numerical example: There are 4 90° elbows (K=0.9), 2 gate valves (K=0.2) and 1 check valve (K=2.0) in a pipeline. If the flow speed V = 2.5 m/s, the total local loss is: ΣK = 4×0.9 + 2×0.2 + 2.0 = 6.0. hl = 6.0 × (2.5²/19.62) = 6.0 × 0.318 = 1.91 m.
Sayısal örnek: Bir boru hattında pitot t: Numerical example: The differential pressure measured with a pitot tube in a pipeline is ΔP = 450 Pa and the fluid is seawater (ρ = 1025 kg/m³). V = √(2 × 450 / 1025) = √(0.878) = 0.937 m/s. If this is measured at the center and the flow is turbulent, the average velocity is corrected to ≈ 0.937 × 0.82 = 0.768 m/s.
Sayısal örnek: Bir yük gemisinde en uzak: Numerical example: A pressure of 0.27 N/mm² (2.7 bar ≈ 27.5 m water column) is required at the farthest hydrant on a cargo ship. If the height difference from the fire pump to the hydrant is 20 m and the pipe friction loss is 8 m, the required pump load is H = 27.5 + 20 + 8 = 55.5 m. If the flow rate is 2 × 120 L/min = 240 L/min = 14.4 m³/h, the pump power P = ρgQH/η = 1025 × 9.81 × (14.4/3600) × 55.5 / 0.65 = 3450 W ≈ 3.5 kW.

Set and drift are two basic parameters used to describe any current (tide, ocean circulation, or wind-induced surface drag) from a marine perspective. The set indicates the direction in which the current is moving (in degrees clockwise from true north, the direction in which the current is traveling); Drift refers to the speed of the current (in nautical miles/hour – knots).

This definition is different from wind direction: while the wind is described from the direction it comes from (e.g. a northwest wind comes from the northwest), the current is described from the direction it goes (e.g. a set 090° current currents east). This difference is especially critical when interpreting current and wind effects in the same calculation.

Ship-Shore Safety Checklist, kâğıt üzeri: Ship-Shore Safety Checklist is not a formality consisting of checking boxes on paper, but a consensus process in which the ship and the terminal mutually verify all critical assumptions of the operation. The list verifies, on a case-by-case basis, that the ship's mooring arrangement is adequate, emergency separation facility (emergency towing-off wire or similar) is available, communications channel and backup are operational, ESD signal is understood by both parties, inert gas system (if applicable) is functioning properly, fire extinguishing equipment is ready for use, and leak/spill response equipment is accessible; Each item is confirmed by the signature of both parties. ISGOTT 6 has transformed this list from a one-time signature formality into a dynamic process that is reconfirmed at regular intervals in long-term transfers, because conditions (weather, ship draft, personnel change) may change during the operation. Omission or superficial filling of the checklist means that both parties operate with different and unverified assumptions about the true state of the operation; This has historically led to serious incidents such as incorrect flow expectations, late detection of a leak, or confusion over who is responsible for ESD. For this reason, terminals do not start transfers until the checklist is completed, and vetting audits also verify that this process has been fully implemented.

Sir Francis Beaufort tarafından 1805'te: The scale, developed by Sir Francis Beaufort in 1805, consists of 13 levels ranging from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane). Each stage corresponds to a specific wind speed range and sea surface signature. For example, Force 4 (11–16 knots) is described as 'small waves become evident and white foam begins to form'. SMC (Safety Management Certificate), ISM: SMC (Safety Management Certificate) links the abstract safety management requirements of the ISM Code into a concrete, auditable document. When a ship carries SMC, it means that it has been verified by external audit that the company's Safety Management System (SMS) is actually installed and operational on that ship. SMC alone is not meaningful: it can only be issued based on a valid DOC (Document of Compliance) of the company. In other words, DOC documents the company's compliance and SMC documents the compliance of each ship; One without the other is invalid. This dual structure ensures that safety is provided simultaneously in both the shore organization and the ship.

SMC (Safety Management Certificate): certifies the ship's compliance with the SMS under the ISM Code. Valid for 5 years.

SMC beş yıl geçerlidir, ancak bu süre bo: SMC is valid for five years, but does not remain inactive during this period: A mandatory intermediate verification is carried out between the 2nd and 3rd year and it is checked that the system is kept alive. Nonconformities found in audits are handled according to their severity; Minor non-conformities are closed within a certain period of time, but a major non-conformity indicates a serious break in the system and if not closed, SMC may be suspended. Without SMC, the ship cannot sail internationally and can lead directly to detention, as ISM non-compliance is one of the most severe categories of deficiencies in PSC. That's why internal audits, DPA communication and management review are conducted continuously.
SMC denetimi (audit) bir belge incelemes: SMC audit is much more than a document review; The auditor looks for 'objective evidence', that is, concrete signs that show that the system is actually implemented as written. In this context, records (drill records, maintenance records, near-miss reports), interviews with the crew and operational observations are evaluated together; For example, it is tested on-site whether a drill has actually been carried out, whether the crew knows their duty in an emergency, or whether critical equipment has been tested. The found non-conformities are classified according to their severity: minor non-conformity is closed within a certain period of time, major non-conformity indicates a serious break in the system and if not closed, SMC may be suspended. Therefore, SMC is the assurance that the ship's safety culture operates in the field, not on paper.

When a new company starts operating or starts operating a new ship type, limited-term (usually 6-12 months) temporary (interim) documents are issued before the required operating history for the full SMC/DOC is established; During this period, it is verified that the system operates under real conditions and then full certification is initiated. Temporary documents also serve as a bridge when the ship owner or operator changes or the flag changes. This mechanism prevents a gap between the establishment of the safety management system and the ship's departure; However, the provisional document requires that minimum elements of the system (DPA assignment, basic procedures, emergency preparedness, basic familiarization of the crew) be available.

SOLAS Chapter IV, GMDSS donanımının bakı: SOLAS Chapter IV requires GMDSS equipment to be maintained by one of three methods (or a combination of several), but this choice is a concrete contractual obligation for the shipowner, not an abstract choice. When shore-based maintenance (SBM) is chosen, the shipowner must sign a formal service agreement with a radio maintenance provider recognized by the flag state and contractually ensure that this provider comes on board at regular intervals (usually annually), testing the equipment, diagnosing faults and replacing parts when necessary; Evidence of this agreement (service certificates, visit reports) may be requested at the audit. When at-sea maintenance (ASM) is selected, the responsibility shifts to the ship's crew: in this case, the relevant officer (usually the second officer or electrical officer) must have received GMDSS maintenance training and the necessary spare parts/test equipment must be on board. The device duplication option compensates for the risk of failure with redundant hardware rather than reducing the maintenance burden. Which of these three methods the shipowner chooses is documented in a DMLC-like format, and the audit questions whether the method chosen is actually implemented (contract, training record or existence of spare equipment); If the chosen method remains on paper, it becomes an irreparable safety gap in case of hardware failure.

Chapter IX mandates the ISM Code, requiring every company to establish a written Safety Management System (SMS), conduct risk assessments, and document continuous improvement. While Chapter XI-1 includes additional measures (IMO number, CSR, ESP) that improve maritime safety, XI-2 regulates ship/port security and security levels with the ISPS Code. Chapter XIV, which mandates the Polar Code, addresses additional risks in polar waters from ice, low temperatures, and remoteness. In drill, for a seafarer, SOLAS is not a collection of rules to be memorized separately; It is a living framework embedded in the daily operation with the survey schedule, certificate validity, drill cycle and equipment maintenance.

SOLAS, denizde insan hayatını korumayı t: SOLAS is an umbrella agreement that aims to protect human life at sea and establishes this with the logic of 'minimum standard'. Its basic philosophy is to ensure that certain safety thresholds are constantly maintained throughout the entire life cycle of a ship, from design to dismantling. The flag state transposes these standards into its own legislation, conducts surveys on behalf of classification societies (RO), and port state control (PSC) comes to the ship as an independent inspection layer. Thanks to this triple structure, there is no dependence on a single control point; Each link of the safety chain controls the other. Another distinctive aspect of SOLAS is the 'tacit acceptance' mechanism: changes come into force automatically unless objected to by a certain date, so the contract remains up to date with technology.

SOLAS, zımni kabul mekanizması sayesinde: Thanks to its tacit acceptance mechanism, SOLAS is constantly evolving and in recent years has gained modern layers that go beyond the classical hardware rules. Goal-Based Standards (GBS) link new shipbuilding rules to target performances to be achieved rather than detailed prescriptions and monitor the compliance of class rules with these targets. Safe Return to Port (SRtP) for cruise ships requires that the ship can return to a safe port under its own power after certain damage or fire and that essential systems continue to operate; thus the ship is designed as 'its own best lifeboat'. Cyber security requirements integrated with the ISM Code make risk management of digital systems (ECDIS, automation, communication) against threats a part of safety management. Therefore, SOLAS compliance for a ship's management is not static: it requires constant monitoring and implementation of MSC circulars and amendments.

It defines the certificates proving the compliance of the ship (Passenger Ship Safety Certificate; Safety Construction, Safety Equipment and Safety Radio certificates for cargo ships) and the types of surveys that verify them: initial, annual, intermediate, periodic and renewal. The Harmonized System of Survey and Certification (HSSC) consolidates surveys of different contracts into a common five-year calendar and windows (±3 months) so that the ship can undergo multiple surveys in a single visit. Somut bir örnek, SOPEP'in gerçekte nasıl: A concrete example shows how SOPEP actually works. When a breach occurs in the hull as a result of a collision between two ships and oil begins to leak into the sea, the first step is to immediately stop cargo or bunker transfer operations; This prevents the leak from growing. The bridge and chief officer then quickly assess the amount of damage and leakage; This assessment forms the basis for all subsequent decisions. Simultaneously, the incident is immediately notified first to the company's onshore office and then to the nearest coastal state, according to the notification chain defined in SOPEP – the timing of this notification is critical not only from an operational but also from a legal perspective, as delayed notification delays the mobilization of response resources and may subsequently aggravate the shipowner's liability. As long as weather and sea conditions are safe, the ship will attempt to limit the spread by spreading its boom around the leak; However, if the sea state or fire risk does not allow this, the response may have to wait until the arrival of regional teams. The speed and correct sequencing in this first hour largely determines whether the pollution reaches the shore.

Sözleşme iki kademeli bir standart tanım: The Convention defines a two-tier standard. D-1 provides for offshore ballast water exchange: at least 200 miles offshore and at a depth of 200 m, at least 95% of the ballast volume is exchanged. This method is a temporary and partial solution because the change is not always fully effective and depends on weather conditions. D-2 is the permanent solution: a Ballast Water Treatment System (BWMS) installed on board reduces the permissible number of living organisms per cubic meter of discharged water to very low limits. The fleet has gradually transitioned from D-1 to D-2 depending on the IOPP renewal survey schedule and this transition is largely complete.

Sözleşme öncesinde her ülke tonajı farkl: Before the convention, each country measured tonnage differently; This led to the same ship being counted as a different 'size' in different ports, resulting in unfair competition. ITC 69 ended this confusion created by the old Moorsom system with a single mathematical framework. GT is linked to the total volume by a logarithmic coefficient, and NT is linked to parameters such as cargo volume, draft/depth ratio and number of passengers. Thus, tonnage is no longer an estimate that varies depending on the measuring authority, but a verifiable calculation result and is documented with the ship's International Tonnage Certificate.

Sözleşmenin kalbi, her koşulda uygulanan: The heart of the contract is Rules 5-8, which apply in all circumstances. Rule 5 mandates keeping a constant and appropriate lookout by eye and ear, as well as by all available means such as radar/AIS. Rule 6 links safe speed to factors such as visibility, traffic density, maneuverability and weather; 'safe speed' is not a fixed number, but the speed at which you can stop and avoid in the current conditions. Rule 7 regulates how the risk of collision is to be assessed (especially the criterion that the compass bearing remains constant), and Rule 8 regulates how the evasive maneuver must be early, obvious and sufficient.
Sözleşmenin özü, 'ya yargıla ya iade et': The essence of the contract is the principle of 'try or extradite' (aut dedere aut judicare). SUA defines in detail what actions are considered crimes and grants jurisdiction to party states based on flag, country or citizenship affiliation. The 2005 Protocol expanded the scope: transporting weapons of mass destruction by sea, using a ship as a weapon and disseminating dangerous substances were also criminalised; In addition, boarding procedures (Article 8bis) have been added, allowing states to stop and search suspicious ships on the high seas with the permission of the flag state.
Sözleşmenin özü, belirlenen zararlı anti: The essence of the convention is the gradual ban of designated harmful antifouling substances. Paints containing TBT are prohibited from first being applied and then kept on board. The contract is not static; The list expands as new evidence emerges: cybutryne (another biocide) has also been added to the list of banned substances, and existing paints have been given a transition period to either seal or remove them. This approach ensures the gradual removal of harmful substances from the sea while giving the industry reasonable time to adapt.
Sözleşmenin pratik omurgası, dünya çapın: The practical backbone of the Convention are the globally recognized standard declaration forms: General Declaration (FAL 1), Cargo Declaration (FAL 2), Store Declaration (FAL 3), Crew Articles Declaration (FAL 4), Crew List (FAL 5), Passenger List (FAL 6) and Dangerous Cargo Manifesto (FAL 7). Thanks to this standardization, the same information does not have to be prepared anew in different formats at each port; The agency and ship management can submit a single data set to different authorities. The Convention also covers humanitarian procedures for stowaway detection, care and repatriation.
Sözleşmenin son bölümleri, gemilerin niy: The final sections of the contract provide for a visual/audible 'reading' of the ships' intentions and status. Part C (Rules 20-31) regulates navigation lights and daytime patterns: the type, size, orientation and particular condition of a ship (at anchor, not under command, towing, fishing, limited manoeuvrability) can only be determined at night from the light pattern. The colors, viewing angles and ranges of the bow light, stern light, sidelights and mast lights are precisely defined. Part D (Kular 32-37) covers audible and visual signals: maneuvering and warning signals (one short blast – turning to starboard, two short – to port, five short – I do not understand your intention/doubt), fog signals in restricted visibility and distress signals. The ability of the officer of the watch to decipher the ship's situation from a beam of light at night and its intention from a sequence of whistles during the day is the basic skill of COLREG in practice.
Sözleşmenin teknik omurgasını iki bölüm: Two parts form the technical backbone of the contract. Chapter II-1 deals with the underwater integrity of the ship: this includes damage stability, watertight bulkheads, double bottoms and the safety of machinery/electrical installations, which ensure that the ship remains afloat when one or more compartments become flooded through subdivision. For ships built after 2009, probabilistic damage stability method is used. Chapter II-2 deals with fire in three stages: prevention (non-flammable materials, containment zones), detection (smoke/heat detectors, manual alarm) and suppression (fixed CO₂/foam/water mist systems, fire circuits). Design of escape routes, fire doors and emergency stop of ventilation are also the subjects of this section.
